questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: How long is the PTE Academic test, and how is it delivered?
o: About 2 hours, computer-based at a test centre
questions.e: PTE Academic is a fully computer-based test taken at a Pearson test centre and lasts about 2 hours. It is never paper-based and cannot be taken at home. The three parts run back-to-back: Speaking & Writing, then Reading, then Listening.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: What score scale does PTE Academic use?
questions.e: PTE Academic reports an overall score and four communicative-skill scores on a 10–90 scale. 0–120 is TOEFL, 1–9 bands is IELTS, 200–800 is TOEIC-style. Your score report shows the overall score plus separate Speaking, Writing, Reading and Listening scores.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: How are PTE Academic responses mainly scored?
o: By automated AI scoring, with human expertise on some tasks
questions.e: PTE Academic is famous for automated scoring: AI engines score speaking and writing against thousands of human-rated responses. Since late 2024, Describe Image and Retell Lecture are double-scored (AI + human review of content), and the newest speaking tasks also involve human scoring. Invigilators never score responses.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: Which are the three parts of PTE Academic, in order?
questions.e: The fixed order is Part 1: Speaking & Writing, Part 2: Reading, Part 3: Listening. Speaking first is deliberate — your voice is warmed up before the mic-heavy section, and several speaking tasks also feed your Reading and Listening scores through integrated scoring.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: Approximately how long is Part 1 (Speaking & Writing)?
questions.e: Speaking & Writing is the longest part at roughly 54–67 minutes. 30–43 minutes is the Listening part; 29–30 minutes is Reading. Because Part 1 is so long and so heavily weighted, most preparation time should go here.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: Which two NEW speaking tasks did Pearson add to PTE Academic on 7 August 2025?
o: Summarize Group Discussion and Respond to a Situation
Write Email and Write from Dictation
questions.e: On 7 August 2025 Pearson added Summarize Group Discussion (SGD) and Respond to a Situation (RTS) to PTE Academic speaking. Both involve human scoring alongside AI, so memorised templates can score zero — natural, relevant answers are required. The other options are long-standing tasks.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: Why do test-takers say 'Speaking is the backbone of PTE'?
o: Speaking tasks also contribute marks to Reading, Listening and Writing through integrated scoring
The speaking section is the longest
questions.e: Many PTE tasks are cross-scored: Read Aloud feeds Speaking + Reading, Repeat Sentence feeds Speaking + Listening, SST feeds Listening + Writing, WFD feeds Listening + Writing. A strong speaking performance therefore lifts three or four skill scores at once. You cannot re-record answers.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: How long are PTE Academic scores valid?
questions.e: PTE Academic scores are valid for 2 years from the test date (the score report shows the validity window). After expiry the score disappears from your account. Some visa pathways reference the score differently, but the report itself is valid two years.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: How quickly do you typically receive PTE Academic results?
questions.e: Pearson states results are typically available within 2 days via your myPTE account — one of PTE's biggest advantages over slower tests. They are not instant, and 13 days is the IELTS paper timeline.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: What does your PTE Score Report show?
o: Overall score plus four communicative-skill scores (10–90 each)
questions.e: The report shows an overall 10–90 score and four separate 10–90 scores for Speaking, Writing, Reading and Listening. There is no pass/fail — institutions set their own minimums (e.g. 58, 65, 79). It also includes a Skills Profile breakdown of task groups.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: What replaced 'Enabling Skills' on the PTE Score Report?
o: The Skills Profile — 8 skill profiles such as Open Response and Reproducing Spoken & Written Language
questions.e: Pearson replaced Enabling Skills with the Skills Profile: 8 profiles (e.g. Open Response Speaking & Writing, Reproducing Spoken & Written Language, Extended/Short Writing, Extended/Short Speaking, Multiple/Single Skill Comprehension). Clicking 'View Skill Profile' shows which task groups pulled your score down — essential for retake planning.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: Which statement about the Personal Introduction is TRUE?
o: It is scored and counts toward Speaking
It is unscored but sent to institutions with your score report
questions.e: The Personal Introduction (25 seconds about yourself) is NOT scored, but the recording is sent to institutions alongside your scores — so speak clearly and professionally. It is mandatory, and it is unscored practice for the mic.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: Approximately how long is the Reading part?
questions.e: Reading is about 29–30 minutes with 13–18 questions. It is the shortest part, and you manage your own time across its five task types — there are no per-question timers.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: Approximately how long is the Listening part?
questions.e: Listening runs 30–43 minutes depending on the question mix (SST items carry 10 minutes each). Like Reading, you manage your own time — except SST's 10-minute timer, which is per item.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: In the August 2025 format, roughly how many tasks does the whole test contain?
questions.e: After the August 2025 update added SGD and RTS, the test has about 22 tasks across the three parts (up from 20). Anyone quoting the old '20 tasks' figure is working from outdated material — check the date on every guide you use.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: Which ID must you bring to the PTE test centre?
o: Any photo ID such as a driving licence
questions.e: You must bring your original, valid passport — the name must match your myPTE registration exactly, and many centres require 3+ months of validity remaining. A driving licence or photocopy will get you turned away as a no-show with no refund.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: What happens if you arrive without an acceptable ID?
o: You take the test and verify ID later
You are marked a no-show and lose the test fee
The centre accepts a digital ID
questions.e: No acceptable ID = no entry = no-show, and the fee (around US$200+–AUD$400+ depending on country) is forfeited. Verify your passport's validity and name spelling days before, not on the morning.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: Which of these contributes to the WRITING score despite sitting in the Listening part?
o: Summarize Spoken Text and Write from Dictation
questions.e: Integrated scoring: SST and WFD sit in Listening but also pay marks into Writing (roughly 18–23% of the writing score each). That is why weak spellers lose Writing points in the Listening section. HIW and SMW do not feed Writing.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: Which speaking tasks feed the READING score?
o: Repeat Sentence and Answer Short Question
Read Aloud (and Highlight Correct Summary feeds Reading from Listening)
questions.e: Read Aloud is cross-scored to Reading (until the 2025 update it was a major donor; it remains a contributor). Highlight Correct Summary in Listening also feeds Reading. RS feeds Listening, not Reading; WFD feeds Listening + Writing.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: What is the '3-second rule' in PTE Speaking?
o: You must start speaking within 3 seconds of the recording starting, or the mic closes
Answers must be exactly 3 seconds long
You get 3 seconds to read each question
Pauses longer than 3 seconds are fine
questions.e: Once recording begins, begin speaking within about 3 seconds — a longer silence and the microphone closes, the item is marked complete, and you score zero for it. This is the single most common technical zero in PTE Speaking.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: What should you do during the 10-minute break between parts?
o: Leave the building for fresh air
Stay in the centre, use the restroom, eat/drink — you cannot access phones or study material
Ask staff about your scores so far
questions.e: There is an optional ~10-minute break after Reading. You may leave the room for the restroom/water, but phones and study materials are prohibited and biometric re-check applies on return. Leaving the building can forfeit your session.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: Which statement about PTE test centres is TRUE?
o: You can choose your seat and neighbour
You sit in a booth with a computer, headset and erasable noteboard; palm-vein scan and photo are taken
You may bring your own laptop
Speaking is done in a separate soundproof room
questions.e: Test centres use individual booths with a computer, headset and erasable noteboard booklet. Identity checks include palm-vein scanning and a photo. Everyone speaks in the same room — expect background noise and keep your own rhythm.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: What is the minimum overall PTE score most Australian student-visa applications reference?
questions.e: Australia's student visa English requirement is commonly cited around PTE 42 overall (requirements change — always check the Department of Home Affairs page before booking). 65 and 79 are typical university and skilled-migration thresholds, not the visa floor.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: A university asks for 'PTE 65 with no band below 58'. What does this mean?
o: Overall 65; each of the four skills at least 58
questions.e: 'No band/skill below X' means every one of the four communicative skills must clear the floor — a 79 in three skills cannot rescue a 50 in the fourth. Fix your weakest skill first; it is the gatekeeper.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: Which is the most heavily weighted SINGLE task type for the overall score?
o: Write from Dictation (each item feeds Listening + Writing with per-word credit)
questions.e: WFD is pound-for-pound the highest-value task: 3–4 items, each scored word-by-word for Listening AND Writing. Missing one WFD item can cost 10+ points across two skills. ASQ and the unscored introduction are low value.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: Why should you ignore 'exam prediction' question banks as your main preparation?
o: Memorised answers fail: content is scored for relevance, and repeated text can be flagged
questions.e: Prediction banks are not illegal and may contain real recalled items, but walking in with memorised answers is dangerous: content scoring checks relevance to the actual prompt, and since late 2024 human reviewers flag templated/generic responses. Use them for practice, not memorisation.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: What does 'integrated skills scoring' mean in PTE?
o: All four skills are tested in one room
Some tasks contribute marks to more than one communicative skill
You can choose which skill a task counts for
questions.e: Integrated scoring means one response can pay into two skills — e.g. Read Aloud → Speaking + Reading, SST → Listening + Writing. It is the structural reason preparation must prioritise high-leverage tasks (WFD, RS, RA, SST) over low-yield ones.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: Which official resource gives you a scored mock with a real score report?
o: Pearson's Official Scored Practice Tests on pearsonpte.com
questions.e: Only Pearson's official Scored Practice Tests (paid, on pearsonpte.com) run the real scoring engine and return an authentic-style report. Free platforms give practice and estimates; YouTube and Reddit give advice, not scores.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: How many times may you retake PTE Academic?
o: As many times as you like
questions.e: There is no limit on PTE retakes — you can rebook as soon as you are ready (and can afford the fee). Retaking to fix one weak skill is legitimate; use the Skills Profile from your last report to target it.

questions.subject: Format & Scoring
questions.q: What should your FIRST preparation step be?
o: Take a diagnostic mock to find your weakest skill, then study the format
questions.e: Diagnose before you drill: a timed mock (ideally an official scored one) reveals whether Speaking, Writing, Reading or Listening is the gatekeeper. Then learn the format task-by-task. Template-memorising first builds the exact habits the 2025–2026 scoring updates punish.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: You get 6–7 Read Aloud items. How much preparation time do you get before the mic opens?
questions.e: Read Aloud gives you roughly 30–40 seconds to read the 50–60-word text silently before recording begins. Use it to mark difficult words, phrase boundaries and stress — never sit idle. Then read for up to 40 seconds.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Read Aloud is scored on which three traits?
questions.e: Every PTE speaking task is scored on Content (all words in correct order, nothing added/omitted), Oral Fluency (rhythm, phrasing, pace) and Pronunciation (sounds intelligible to most English speakers). Grammar/vocabulary/spelling are writing traits, not speaking traits.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: You mispronounce a word mid-sentence. What is the highest-scoring recovery?
o: Stop, go back and re-read the sentence
Keep going without pausing — fluency damage from a stop hurts more
questions.e: Never stop or backtrack: corrections count as added words (hurting Content) and the hesitation craters Fluency. One mispronounced word costs a little; a 2-second stall plus a repeated phrase costs a lot. Keep moving forward.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: What pace should you aim for in Read Aloud?
o: As fast as possible to show fluency
Faster on easy words, slow on hard ones
questions.e: The AI rewards natural rhythm: steady pace, correct phrasing, sentence stress. Racing causes stumbles; crawling sounds hesitant. Read it like a newsreader — smooth and even, not like a race or a spelling test.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: How should you handle commas and full stops while reading?
o: Ignore them — punctuation is visual only
Pause briefly at commas, slightly longer at full stops
questions.e: Short pause at commas, longer at full stops — this is 'phrasing', and it is exactly what the fluency engine measures. Ignoring punctuation produces run-on monotone; pausing too long triggers hesitation penalties.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: A text contains the word 'colonel'. You have 5 seconds before the mic opens. What do you do?
o: Recall it is pronounced 'kernel' and say it correctly
questions.e: Use prep time to decode traps: colonel → 'kernel', choir → 'kwire', yacht → 'yot'. Reading letter-by-letter ('col-o-nel') damages both Content and Pronunciation; skipping deletes a content word. Never whisper — the mic needs clear volume.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Which habit most damages Oral Fluency in Read Aloud?
o: Frequent 'um', repetitions and long mid-sentence pauses
questions.e: Fillers, false starts, repetitions and hesitations are what the fluency algorithm detects — a regional accent does not, as long as sounds are intelligible. Fluency is about smoothness, not accent elimination.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: How should numbers like '3,400' and '25%' be read?
questions.e: Read numbers as words: 3,400 → 'three thousand four hundred', 25% → 'twenty-five percent'. Reading symbols literally ('percent sign') or skipping numbers loses Content marks — numbers are content words like any other.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: During the 30–40 second preparation, what is the BEST use of your time?
o: Rehearse the first sentence only, perfectly
Silently read the whole text, marking hard words and phrase breaks
Plan what to do after the test
questions.e: One full silent pass lets you decode hard words and chunk the text into phrases — the two things that prevent stumbles. Perfecting only the first sentence leaves the rest unmapped; relaxing wastes the only advantage the task gives you.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: The mic opens but you are not ready. What should you do?
o: Start speaking within ~3 seconds even if imperfectly
questions.e: The 3-second rule: silence longer than ~3 seconds closes the microphone and the item scores zero. An imperfect start beats a perfect silence. Always begin on time — fluency can recover, a closed mic cannot.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Which of these counts as an ADDED word hurting your Content score?
questions.e: Content = every word in the text, in order, no additions, no omissions. A stumbled repeat ('the the') is an added word; a self-correction inserts extra words too. Pauses and pace do not affect Content — only the word sequence does.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Your text has an unfamiliar long word: 'photosynthesis'. Best approach?
o: Sound it out syllable by syllable confidently: pho-to-syn-the-sis
questions.e: Break long words into syllables and say them steadily — most English words are decodable this way, and confident syllable-by-syllable delivery preserves fluency. Mumbling, substituting or pausing all damage Content or Fluency more.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: How does sentence stress help your Pronunciation score?
o: It doesn't — only individual sounds matter
Stressing content words (nouns, main verbs) with natural rhythm makes speech intelligible
Stress only the last word of each sentence
questions.e: English is stress-timed: the AI's pronunciation model expects content words stressed and grammar words reduced. Flat, equal stress on every word sounds robotic and less intelligible; natural stress patterns are what 'good pronunciation' means to the engine.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Should you imitate a British or American accent for a higher score?
o: No — any accent is fine if easily understood
questions.e: Pearson is explicit: all standard accents are accepted; the engine scores intelligibility, not accent type. Chasing a fake native accent usually wrecks fluency — speak clearly in your own accent.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: What is the ideal recording length for a Read Aloud text?
o: Roughly 30–40 seconds — the full text at natural pace
questions.e: Read the complete text once at natural pace — typically 30–40 seconds for a 50–60-word passage. Finishing in 10 seconds means you skipped content; the recorder cuts at 40 seconds, so dawdling truncates your ending.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: A classmate says: 'Read Aloud is easy marks — just read fast.' What is wrong?
o: Speed causes stumbles, skipped words and monotone delivery, hurting all three traits
questions.e: Racing is the classic RA trap: it produces misread words (Content), stumbles (Fluency) and slurred sounds (Pronunciation). The task rewards newsreader-steady delivery, and since 2025 it feeds only Speaking — there is no Reading safety net left to subsidise sloppy reading.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Since the August 2025 scoring update, Read Aloud contributes to:
o: Speaking and Reading equally, as before
Speaking only — the Reading donation was removed
questions.e: The 2025 update made Read Aloud a single-skill (Speaking-only) task — it no longer donates points to Reading. This is the 'Read Aloud Trap': students who relied on RA to carry Reading now fall 1–2 points short and must earn Reading marks from fill-in-the-blanks instead.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Which preparation drill best improves Read Aloud?
o: Shadowing: listen to a native speaker and repeat simultaneously, then read aloud daily with a timer
questions.e: Shadowing trains the exact muscles RA needs — chunking, stress, pace — and daily timed read-alouds build stamina. Memorising passages cannot transfer to unseen texts; silent reading trains nothing the mic hears.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: The text includes 'Dr. Smith (born 1962) discovered...'. How do you read 'Dr.' and '(born 1962)'?
o: 'Doctor Smith, born nineteen sixty-two, discovered' — read abbreviations and parenthetical content naturally
questions.e: Expand abbreviations (Dr. → 'Doctor', e.g. → 'for example') and read parenthetical dates as words ('nineteen sixty-two'). Skipping them deletes content words; spelling out 'D-R' or saying 'bracket' inserts wrong words.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: What does 'chunking' or 'meaningful clusters' mean in Read Aloud?
o: Reading one word at a time
Grouping words into natural phrases (e.g. 'The results of the study / were published / last year')
questions.e: Chunking = phrasing words into meaning groups, the 2026-evolved version of the old 'one-line strategy'. It protects fluency (you pause at boundaries, not mid-phrase) and aids pronunciation (stress lands on the right words). Word-by-word reading destroys both.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Your neighbour starts speaking loudly during your Read Aloud. You should:
o: Keep your pace and volume steady — the headset mic is noise-cancelling
questions.e: The headset microphone is directional and noise-cancelling; stopping or shouting both damage your scores. Test centres are noisy by design — train with background noise so exam-day chatter does not break your rhythm.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Which of these is a legitimate way to use the erasable noteboard during Read Aloud prep?
o: Mark stress on 2–3 tricky words and draw phrase breaks (/)
It cannot be used in this task
questions.e: Quick marks — slashes for phrase breaks, underlines for stressed syllables — turn prep time into a delivery map. Copying the whole text wastes the 30 seconds; the board is allowed in every task.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: True or False: you may re-record a Read Aloud answer if you stumble.
o: False — one attempt only; the item advances automatically
False — you must skip the item
questions.e: Every PTE speaking item is single-attempt: when you stop speaking (or the timer ends), the item closes and the test advances. There is no re-record button — which is why the 'never stop, never backtrack' rule matters.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: A 60-word text, 40 seconds recording time. You finish in 22 seconds. Likely cause?
o: You skipped words or sentences — Content loss
questions.e: 60 words at natural pace takes ~30–35 seconds. Finishing in 22 means whole phrases went missing (or you raced and slurred). If you finish early with time left, you almost certainly dropped content — check skipped lines in practice.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Which breathing technique helps Read Aloud delivery?
o: Hold your breath for the whole passage
Breathe at punctuation boundaries during prep-marked pauses
questions.e: Plan breaths at commas and full stops — the same boundaries where fluency pauses belong. Gasping mid-phrase breaks a chunk and sounds hesitant; holding your breath starves the end of the passage of air and volume.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: The single biggest Read Aloud score killer for most test-takers is:
o: Hesitations, repetitions and self-corrections breaking fluency
questions.e: Fluency breaks — ums, repeats, restarts, long pauses — are what the engine penalises most heavily, and they usually come from racing or zero prep. Accent is not scored against you; quiet delivery only matters if the mic cannot hear you.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: In Repeat Sentence you hear a sentence of about 3–9 seconds. What is the proven listening method?
o: Listen for meaning in 2–3 chunks and echo the phrasing, then repeat fluently
Write the full sentence on the noteboard
Repeat each word the moment you hear it
questions.e: Chunking beats word-memorising: grasp the sentence as 2–3 meaning phrases ('Next week's tutorial / on Tuesday / has been cancelled'), hold the meaning, and reproduce it fluently. Writing the full sentence splits attention (Pearson advises keeping it in your head); shadowing aloud trains nothing since you cannot speak during playback.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Repeat Sentence is scored on Content, Fluency and Pronunciation. How is Content measured?
o: Number of correct words in the correct sequence
questions.e: Content = correct word sequences: each word you reproduce in the right order earns credit (partial credit applies — 50% of the words right still scores). Understanding the topic helps memory but is not scored directly; adding fancy synonyms for forgotten words scores zero for those slots.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: You remember the sentence except one middle word. Best strategy?
o: Freeze until the word comes back
Keep the flow: say the parts you remember fluently, inserting a neutral filler-free continuation
Stay silent — a wrong word is worse
questions.e: Partial credit rewards every correct word in sequence, and fluency rewards unbroken delivery. Freezing sacrifices both; silence scores nothing. Say what you caught, smoothly — 'The new policy will take [gap] at the beginning of next year' still earns most of the marks.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: How many Repeat Sentence items appear, and what do they feed?
questions.e: Expect 10–12 Repeat Sentence items — the highest-count speaking task — each feeding both Speaking and Listening. That double contribution is why RS is the #1 priority task for most score plans.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Which note-taking approach works for Repeat Sentence?
o: First letters of content words, or nothing — full notes divide attention
Drawing the sentence as a picture
questions.e: If you write at all, jot first letters of key words — full transcription makes you miss the audio's second half. Many 90-scorers take no notes and rely on chunked echoic memory. Never let note-taking compete with listening.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: The speaker has an unfamiliar accent. What should you do?
o: Panic — accents are not in the test
Focus on stressed content words and sentence rhythm; meaning carries across accents
questions.e: PTE deliberately uses varied accents. Content words (nouns, main verbs) carry the meaning and are stressed in every accent; locking onto them plus the rhythm lets you reconstruct the sentence. There are no replays — every item plays once.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Describe Image gives you 25 seconds to study the image and 40 seconds to speak. What is scored?
questions.e: Same three speaking traits: Content = describing the image's actual key features (trends, highs/lows, categories), Fluency and Pronunciation as usual. There is no 'template' trait — and since late 2024, rigid memorised templates are flagged by human reviewers and can tank the score.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Since November 2024, what happens to rigid 30-word memorised Describe Image templates?
o: They are flagged by human reviewers and can score near zero for content
questions.e: Pearson added human review of Describe Image and Retell Lecture content: generic filler that fits any image ('the given image represents beautiful image...') is flagged as templated and can score zero for Content. Use a flexible structure filled with the image's real data, not a memorised script.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: What is the recommended flexible structure for Describe Image?
o: Introduction (image type + topic) → key features/trends → highest and lowest values → conclusion
Read the title, then stay silent
questions.e: The 2026-safe structure: 1) image type + topic, 2) 2–3 key features or trends, 3) highest/lowest values, 4) one-line conclusion — every slot filled with THIS image's data. It is a framework, not a script: the words change with the image, so it passes human review.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: During the 25-second Describe Image preparation, prioritise:
o: Identifying the topic, 2–3 key numbers/trends, and the highest/lowest values
Planning a joke to sound natural
questions.e: 25 seconds is enough for: topic + 2–3 key figures + max/min. Trying to capture everything guarantees a rushed, hesitant delivery. Fluency rewards selecting a few features and describing them smoothly over reciting a data dump.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: The image is a process diagram (e.g. water cycle). Your description should emphasise:
o: The stages in sequence with linking words (first, then, finally)
questions.e: Process/cycle diagrams are about sequence: walk through the stages in order using linkers. Bar/line/pie charts are about comparisons and max/min. Matching your structure to the image type is what 'relevant content' means — opinions and colours are irrelevant.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: You run out of things to say with 10 seconds left in Describe Image. Best move?
o: Elaborate: compare two categories, restate the trend differently, add the conclusion
questions.e: Never surrender time to silence — fluency is scored across the whole 40 seconds. Develop: compare categories, rephrase a trend, restate max/min, conclude. Verbatim repetition and 'um'-filling both read as disfluency to the engine.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: For a bar chart, which detail is usually LEAST worth your limited seconds?
o: The exact value of every single bar
questions.e: Describe Image rewards selection, not transcription: highest, lowest and trend carry the content marks; reciting all twelve bars eats your 40 seconds and sounds like reading, not describing. Round numbers ('about 40 percent') — relevance beats precision.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: True or False: rounding numbers (e.g. 'around 35%') is acceptable in Describe Image.
o: True — relevance and fluency beat decimal precision
True — but only for pie charts
questions.e: The scoring guide values relevant content delivered fluently; nobody is checking your arithmetic. 'Approximately 35 percent' keeps you fluent where 'thirty-four point seven percent' trips you. Save exactness for Write from Dictation, where every word counts.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Which opening is safest for ANY Describe Image in 2026?
o: 'The given image represents beautiful image and there must have been a popular debate...'
questions.e: A factual, image-specific opening ('The bar chart compares urban and rural internet access between 2015 and 2025') states type + topic and flows into data. Option A is the infamous flagged template — memorised filler that human reviewers now zero. Personal opinions waste content time.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: How should you practise Repeat Sentence daily for maximum gain?
o: Listen to 10–15 sentences, chunk-repeat them aloud immediately, tracking words-correct
questions.e: Deliberate RS practice = listen once → repeat aloud at once → count exact words right. 10–15 reps daily builds the chunk-and-echo muscle the task tests. Silent reading and subtitled movies do not train immediate oral reproduction.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: In Describe Image, what does 'relevance beats accuracy' mean?
o: Describing the right features fluently outscores stumbling over precise figures
Accuracy does not matter at all
Only describe what you are sure of, even if trivial
questions.e: It means prioritise: the main trend and key comparisons delivered smoothly beat a hesitant recitation of exact decimals. It does NOT mean inventing data — fabricated numbers are irrelevant content and score zero for those stretches.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Which of these is a content error in Describe Image?
o: Saying values rose when the chart shows they fell
questions.e: Content = accurate, relevant description. Reversing a trend is factually wrong content; linkers, full use of time and citing the title are all good practice. Human reviewers specifically check that your words match the image.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: For Repeat Sentence, why is copying the speaker's stress and intonation useful?
o: Rhythm and stress patterns act as memory hooks for the next phrase
questions.e: Prosody is a retrieval cue: remembering the sentence as a sound pattern ('da-DA-da-da DA') triggers the words that rode on it. This is the 'mental echoing' technique — you are not scored on mimicking the speaker, but the rhythm helps you reproduce the words that ARE scored.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: You have practised Describe Image with a fixed template for months. With the 2026 rules, you should:
o: Keep it — old habits are comfortable
Convert it to a flexible framework: same structure, but every sentence carries this image's real data
Use the template only for pie charts
questions.e: Structure is still essential — rambling fails too. The fix is flexibility: keep the 4-block skeleton (intro → features → max/min → conclusion) but generate the content fresh per image. Reviewers flag repeated identical phrasing across items, not organised answers.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Which image type is generally considered hardest, and why?
o: Picture/photo with no data — you must infer and describe elements without numbers to lean on
questions.e: Data-free pictures (a photo of a landscape, a building) remove the numbers crutch: you must describe elements, positions and possible implications fluently. Practise these deliberately — describe foreground/background, notable features, and a concluding observation.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: A good 40-second Describe Image typically contains how many words?
questions.e: At natural pace (~140–160 wpm), 40 seconds ≈ 90–110 words — roughly 6–8 sentences. 30 words means long silences (fluency collapse); 200 means racing (stumbles). Time your practice answers: structure first, then fill to ~100 words.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: In Repeat Sentence, the sentence is: 'The chemistry building is closed for renovation this semester.' You say: 'The chemistry building is closed for renovation this year.' What happens?
o: You lose the final word's content credit; 'semester' → 'year' scores zero for that slot
questions.e: Content is scored per word-sequence: 'year' for 'semester' is simply a wrong word in that slot — you keep credit for the 9 correct words. One wrong word never zeroes a sentence; that is why attempting the full sentence always beats freezing.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: What is 'rhythmic monotony' and why does it matter in 2026?
o: Identical unnatural rhythm across answers — flagged as template use by reviewers
questions.e: Reviewers watch for answers that sound metronomic-identical across items — the fingerprint of a memorised template recited regardless of content. Vary your connectors and sentence shapes naturally; genuine answers have natural rhythmic variety.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Best describe-image drill for the 25-second prep?
o: 25-second sprint: say aloud 'type, topic, 2 numbers, max, min' — then deliver
questions.e: Train the sprint: in 25 seconds, extract type + topic + 2–3 figures + max/min, then speak. Writing a script is impossible in the time and reading it aloud sounds robotic. The sprint builds the selection reflex the task rewards.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Which statement about Describe Image timing is TRUE?
o: You can extend to 60 seconds by speaking fast
25s prep + 40s speaking; the mic cuts at 40s and 3s of silence ends it early
You get 40s prep and 25s to speak
questions.e: Fixed: 25 seconds to study, 40 seconds to speak. The recorder stops at 40 seconds; 3+ seconds of silence closes it early. Reversing the numbers is a common confusion — prep is shorter than delivery.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Your Repeat Sentence recall is weak. Which underlying skill should you train?
o: Short-term auditory memory via chunking and shadowing exercises
questions.e: RS is a memory task wearing a speaking mask: training = chunking drills, shadowing, and immediate oral repetition of 8–14-word sentences. Reading/typing speed is irrelevant — nothing is read or typed in this task.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Retell Lecture: you hear a 60–90 second lecture, get 10 seconds to prepare, then speak for up to 40 seconds. What is the note-taking rule?
o: Capture key nouns, numbers and relationships — notes are triggers, not transcripts
questions.e: You cannot transcribe 90 seconds of speech — trying means missing the next idea. Capture triggers: key nouns, numbers, cause→effect links, roughly one short line per 15–20 seconds. In your 40 seconds you expand triggers into fluent sentences.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: What is the best Retell Lecture delivery structure?
o: 'The lecture was about [topic]. Firstly... Furthermore... In conclusion...' using your notes
Give your opinion of the lecture
questions.e: A simple spine — topic sentence + 3–4 linked points + closing line — turns scattered notes into a coherent 40-second retell. Opinions are irrelevant content; random order sounds disfluent even if the words are right.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Retell Lecture feeds which scores?
questions.e: Retell Lecture is cross-scored to Speaking and Listening — understanding the lecture (Listening) and reproducing it (Speaking). Like Describe Image, its content is now double-scored by AI + human reviewers, so generic filler fails.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: During the 10-second Retell Lecture prep time, you should:
o: Glance at your notes, pick your topic sentence and 3 points, then start within 3 seconds of the beep
questions.e: 10 seconds = select, not create: choose the topic line and your 3 strongest points, then launch promptly (3-second rule applies). Writing more notes or full rehearsal wastes the window — you will think while speaking, using the structure as rails.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: You understood only ~40% of the lecture. Best approach?
o: Stay silent — wrong content is penalised
Retell the 40% fluently and confidently with a clear structure
questions.e: Partial content delivered fluently still earns Content marks for what is right plus full Fluency/Pronunciation. Silence earns zero everything; invented details are irrelevant content that human reviewers penalise. Never surrender the 40 seconds.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Which note-taking layout works best for Retell Lecture?
o: Topic at top, then 3–4 short lines with arrows for cause→effect and +/− for contrasts
questions.e: Structured triggers: topic header, then telegraphic lines with arrows showing relationships. In delivery you read a line and expand it into a sentence. Paragraphs and full sentences cannot be scanned in the 10-second prep.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Answer Short Question: the audio asks a question; you have 10 seconds to answer. What response format scores?
o: One word or a short phrase — no full sentence needed
A question back to the examiner
questions.e: ASQ wants a short, correct response — usually a single word or phrase ('Eyes', 'A thermometer'). Full sentences waste your 10 seconds and add words the scorer must sift. Content is all that matters here; fluency is barely tested in a one-word answer.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: ASQ: 'What do you call the frozen form of water?' The correct response is:
o: Very cold water that becomes hard in winter
questions.e: ASQ answers are short and literal: 'Ice'. Snow is a different thing (frozen precipitation), steam is the gas form. Do not dress up a one-word answer — the scorer matches vocabulary, not eloquence.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: ASQ: 'Which instrument is used to measure temperature?'
questions.e: A thermometer measures temperature; a barometer measures air pressure, a ruler measures length, a compass shows direction. ASQ is general-knowledge vocabulary — the fix for misses is word-list study, not technique.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: ASQ: 'What is the name of the red planet?'
questions.e: Mars is the red planet. This is the ASQ pattern: common knowledge + precise vocabulary. Build a 200-word ASQ word bank (planets, instruments, occupations, body parts) — misses here are pure vocabulary gaps.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: ASQ: 'What do we call a person who treats animals?'
questions.e: 'Veterinarian' (or 'vet') is the precise term; 'doctor' is too general for the scorer's expected vocabulary. ASQ rewards the exact word — near-synonyms often fail because the answer key matches specific vocabulary.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: ASQ: 'How many days are there in a leap year?'
questions.e: 366 — the February 29th year. ASQ mixes vocabulary with quick facts; hesitation here usually means the knowledge is missing, not the English. Drill common ASQ facts (days, months, directions, simple science) until instant.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: ASQ: 'What organ do we use to breathe?'
questions.e: The lungs. Note the singular/plural trap many learners hit: 'lung' alone is marked wrong by strict keys — the expected form is 'lungs'. Learn ASQ answers in their natural number (glasses, scissors, lungs, eyes).

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: ASQ: 'Which direction does the sun rise?'
questions.e: East. ASQ is 10–12 rapid items testing instant vocabulary and facts — each worth little alone, but collectively they are free marks for anyone with the word bank. Answer in the first 2–3 seconds; do not deliberate.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: ASQ: 'What do you call a doctor who treats children?'
questions.e: 'Paediatrician' (pediatrician) is the precise term. ASQ loves occupation vocabulary — paediatrician, veterinarian, astronaut, librarian, florist. A general word like 'doctor' misses the expected key.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: ASQ: 'What is the opposite of 'expand'?'
questions.e: 'Contract' is the direct antonym. ASQ includes antonym/synonym items — keep an opposites list (expand/contract, ancient/modern, scarce/abundant). 'Extend' and 'enlarge' are synonyms of expand, the classic distractor trap.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: ASQ: 'Which month has the fewest days?'
questions.e: February (28, or 29 in leap years). Calendar items are ASQ staples. Say just 'February' — adding 'the month of' wastes time and adds unscored words.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: ASQ: 'What do we measure with a clock?'
questions.e: Time. Instrument→quantity mapping is a whole ASQ sub-category: clock→time, scale→weight, thermometer→temperature, speedometer→speed. Learn them as pairs and these items become automatic.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: How many Answer Short Question items appear, and what is each worth?
o: 10–12 items; small individually but free marks in aggregate
questions.e: ASQ runs ~10–12 quick items feeding Speaking (+Listening). Each is worth little, but a prepared candidate banks them all in two minutes — the best marks-per-minute ratio in the test. Unprepared candidates donate them.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: In Retell Lecture, why must you NOT give your opinion?
o: Content = the lecture's ideas; your opinions are irrelevant content the scorer cannot match
questions.e: The scorer matches your words against the lecture's content — your views on the topic match nothing and earn nothing, while consuming fluency time. Retell = report, not review. Save opinions for the essay.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Which phrase BEST opens a Retell Lecture response?
o: 'I think the lecture was interesting because...'
questions.e: A crisp topic sentence with the actual subject ('The lecture discussed urban heat islands, focusing on causes and mitigation') banks content immediately and launches fluency. Opinions, greetings and fillers waste the highest-attention seconds of your answer.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: For ASQ preparation, what is the highest-yield activity?
o: Drilling a 200–300 item ASQ question bank until answers are instant
questions.e: ASQ is 90% instant recall of common vocabulary/facts — a drilled question bank makes answers reflexive. Essays and movies do not build one-word retrieval speed; templates are irrelevant to one-word answers.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Retell Lecture: the lecture lists three causes of coral bleaching. You caught two. You should:
o: Describe only one in great depth
Present the two fluently, linked, with a concluding line
List them as bullet words with long pauses
questions.e: Two causes delivered as connected, fluent sentences ('Firstly... Furthermore...') earn strong content + fluency. One cause padded thin wastes time; pretending the count was two is inaccurate; pausing between bare words destroys fluency.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: What do Describe Image, Retell Lecture, SGD and RTS now share (2025–2026)?
o: Human reviewers check content alongside AI — generic memorised answers are penalised
They all use the same template
questions.e: The 2025–2026 scoring evolution: these productive speaking tasks are now double-scored (AI + human content review). The common thread is that authentic, prompt-specific content is mandatory — the era of one-template-fits-all speaking ended in November 2024.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: ASQ: 'What do you call the written text of a play?'
questions.e: 'Script' is the precise term for a play's text. ASQ art/literature items (script, novel, biography, portrait, landscape) reward exact genre vocabulary — 'play text' would miss the key.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: ASQ: 'Which organ pumps blood around the body?'
questions.e: The heart. Body-part ASQs are frequent and strict on number: 'hearts' would be wrong, 'heart' alone is acceptable here since the key expects the singular organ name — learn each item's expected form from a real bank.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: Summarize Written Text gives you one passage and 10 minutes. What must your response be?
questions.e: SWT = exactly one sentence, 5–75 words, in 10 minutes. Two sentences (even joined by 'and') fails the form requirement and scores zero. 200–300 words is the essay; 50–70 words is SST.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: SWT is scored on Form, Grammar, Vocabulary and Content. What does FORM check?
questions.e: Form = one sentence, 5–75 words. Write two sentences or 4 words and Form = 0, which caps the whole item regardless of brilliant content. Always count your words before submitting — the word counter is on screen.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: What is the most reliable SWT method?
o: Write from memory without looking back
Extract 3–4 key points, join with connectors (while, although, because, which) into one long grammatical sentence
Copy the first and last sentences of the passage
Summarise in your own words without key terms
questions.e: The join method: pull 3–4 key points (usually one per paragraph), then stitch them with subordinating connectors into one 40–60-word sentence. Copying whole sentences risks plagiarism-style penalties and misses points; pure paraphrase without key terms loses Content.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: Which connectors are ideal for joining SWT points into one sentence?
o: While, although, because, which, whereas, despite
questions.e: Subordinating connectors (while, although, because, which, whereas, despite, since) merge clauses into ONE grammatical sentence — exactly what Form demands. 'And'-chains sound childish; 'firstly/secondly' signal multiple sentences and break form.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: Your SWT draft is 82 words. What should you do?
o: Trim to under 75 words by cutting adjectives and examples
Delete the whole thing and restart
questions.e: Over 75 words = Form zero. Trim ruthlessly: cut examples, adjectives and repeated ideas until 40–60 words. Two sentences also zeroes Form. Aim for the 50–60 sweet spot — safely inside the range with room for all key points.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: Your SWT draft is 4 words: 'Pollution harms marine life.' What is wrong?
o: Under 5 words = Form zero; expand with 2–3 key points from the passage
questions.e: Form requires minimum 5 words — 4 words scores zero no matter how true. Expand by adding the passage's key points (causes, effects, solutions) joined with connectors. Never submit a one-liner in SWT.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: How should you spend the 10 minutes in SWT?
o: ~2 min reading and extracting key points, ~6 min writing, ~2 min checking form/grammar/spelling
questions.e: Budget: 2 minutes to read and mark key points, 6 to compose the single sentence, 2 to verify (one sentence? 5–75 words? verbs agree? spelling?). Writing blind for 10 minutes produces form errors; thinking for 9 leaves no writing time.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: Which sentence would FAIL SWT form?
o: 'Industrial pollution damages marine ecosystems, although regulations have reduced emissions since 2010.'
'Industrial pollution damages marine ecosystems. Regulations have reduced emissions since 2010.'
'Although regulations have reduced emissions since 2010, industrial pollution continues to damage marine ecosystems.'
'Industrial pollution, which damages marine ecosystems, has declined where regulations tightened since 2010.'
questions.e: Option B is two sentences — Form zero, even though the content is fine. A, C and D are each ONE sentence using subordination. The period is the enemy: one full stop only, at the very end.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: What is the ideal SWT length?
questions.e: 40–60 words is the sweet spot: room for 3–4 key points with safe margins from both limits. Hugging 75 risks a miscount tipping you over; 5 words leaves content uncovered. Quality of coverage beats word-count brinkmanship.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: In SWT, what does the CONTENT trait reward?
o: Covering the passage's key points accurately
questions.e: Content = key points captured: the scorer compares your sentence against the passage's main ideas. Fancy synonyms for no reason and personal opinions add nothing — and opinions actively hurt, since they are not in the passage.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: Should you copy phrases from the passage in SWT?
o: Copy key terms and noun phrases, but build the sentence yourself
questions.e: Key terms (names, technical nouns) SHOULD be reused — paraphrasing 'photosynthesis' into something vague loses content. But the sentence structure must be yours; lifting whole sentences is penalised. Borrow bricks, build your own house.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: Which error is most common in SWT grammar?
o: Subject-verb disagreement in long joined sentences ('pollution... have')
questions.e: Long single sentences breed agreement errors: writers lose track of the subject across clauses ('pollution... have increased'). Check every verb against its subject in your 2-minute review. Spelling variant (British/American) is fine if consistent.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: The passage discusses causes, effects AND solutions. Your summary covers only causes. Result?
o: Full content marks — causes are most important
Partial content — each aspect is a key point you missed
questions.e: Content is proportional: each major aspect (causes, effects, solutions) is a scorable key point. Covering one of three caps your content at roughly a third. Extract one point per aspect — that is why the 3–4-point method works.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: How many SWT items appear in the test?
questions.e: Only 1–2 SWT items — but each feeds both Writing and Reading, and 10 minutes each makes them time-expensive. They are quality-over-quantity tasks: one perfect sentence beats three rushed ones (which you will never get to write).

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: Which is the best SWT checking routine before submitting?
o: Count: one full stop? 5–75 words? Then scan verbs, articles and spelling
questions.e: The 2-minute check: exactly one sentence (one full stop), word count in range, subject-verb agreement, articles (a/an/the), spelling of key terms. This catches the form-killers and grammar slips that separate 65 from 79.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: What does 'key point extraction' mean in SWT practice?
o: Reading each paragraph and writing its main idea in 5–6 words
questions.e: Extraction drill: per paragraph, jot the main idea in a few words ('para 1: plastic kills turtles'). These jottings become your 3–4 joined points. Highlighting everything highlights nothing; memorising wastes the 10 minutes.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: A student writes SWT summaries of 30 words covering 2 points and scores 55 in Writing. The likely fix?
o: Expand to 45–60 words covering 3–4 points — content coverage is the gap
questions.e: 30 words / 2 points = thin content. The scorer wants the passage's key ideas; adding the missing points (effects, solutions) with connectors lifts Content without touching anything else. Vocabulary is rarely the SWT bottleneck — coverage is.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: Which word-counting mistake is dangerous in SWT?
o: Forgetting the on-screen word counter exists and submitting blind
questions.e: The screen shows a live word counter — submitting without glancing at it is how 76-word and 2-sentence answers happen. Trust the counter, not your estimate. (Hyphenation edge cases are trivial next to a blind submit.)

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: True or False: SWT also contributes to your Reading score.
o: True — it is cross-scored to Reading
questions.e: SWT sits in the Writing section but pays into Reading too — summarising a text demonstrates reading comprehension. This double value is why SWT deserves full preparation despite having only 1–2 items.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: Which opening clause works for most SWT responses?
o: A noun-phrase subject capturing the topic: 'The passage argues that...' is weak — better: 'Rising plastic pollution...'
questions.e: Start with the topic as subject ('Rising plastic pollution threatens marine life, although...') — content from word one. 'The passage argues' wastes words meta-commenting; opinions ('I agree') add unscored content. (The option text itself notes the weaker variant — lead with substance.)

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: Your best SWT practice routine is:
o: 3 passages a week: extract points, write the sentence, verify form + word count, compare against key points
questions.e: Deliberate reps: extract → compose → verify (form/count) → check coverage against the passage's key points. Typing speed is irrelevant at 50 words; reading others' summaries skips the composing muscle the task tests.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: If the passage is highly technical (e.g. quantum computing), you should:
o: Reuse its key technical terms and summarise the relationships (what does what)
Simplify all terms into everyday words
questions.e: Technical terms are content anchors — reuse them ('quantum bits', 'superposition') and describe what the passage says they DO. 'Simplifying' them into vague words ('tiny things') destroys content. You are summarising, not translating.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: The Write Essay task requires:
questions.e: Essay = 200–300 words, 20 minutes. Under 120 or over 380 words scores zero — the form window is strict. 50–70 words is SST; one sentence is SWT. Two essay tasks appear per test (since the late-2025 format change).

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: What is the recommended essay structure?
o: Introduction (paraphrase + thesis) → 2 body paragraphs (point + example each) → conclusion
questions.e: The 4-paragraph structure: intro (paraphrase prompt + clear position), two body paragraphs (topic sentence + explanation + example), conclusion (restate position). It satisfies Content, Coherence and Form simultaneously — and it is fast to execute under 20 minutes.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: How should you spend the 20 minutes?
o: ~3 min planning, ~14 min writing, ~3 min checking
questions.e: 3-14-3: plan (position + 2 points + examples), write (~250 words), check (word count, grammar, spelling, one idea per paragraph). Zero planning produces rambling; zero checking leaves form/grammar marks on the table.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: What is the ideal essay length?
questions.e: 230–260 words: comfortably inside the 200–300 window with full development of two body paragraphs. 120 risks thin content; 380+ risks the zero-word-count penalty and error multiplication. More words = more chances to err.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: Which thesis statement is strongest?
o: 'While technology brings challenges, its benefits for education outweigh the drawbacks.'
questions.e: A strong thesis takes a clear position and previews the argument ('benefits outweigh drawbacks'). 'Will discuss' promises nothing; 'good and bad' is fence-sitting; disclaimers destroy credibility. The scorer rewards a clear, developed position.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: What counts as good 'development' in a body paragraph?
o: Topic sentence → explanation of the mechanism → concrete example
questions.e: Development = claim, mechanism, evidence: state the point, explain HOW/WHY it works, ground it with a concrete example. Repetition and bare anecdotes do not develop; rhetorical questions develop nothing.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: Which linking devices help Coherence & Cohesion?
o: 'Moreover, however, consequently, for instance, in contrast'
questions.e: Academic linkers signal relationships: addition (moreover), contrast (however), cause (consequently), example (for instance). Fillers ('um') and 'and then' chains mark spoken, not written, register. Variety matters — do not start every sentence with 'Moreover'.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: What is the essay's biggest vocabulary trap?
o: Forcing memorised 'fancy' words incorrectly ('the deleterious ramifications proliferate')
questions.e: Misused fancy vocabulary ('big words used wrongly') damages the Vocabulary trait more than simple correct words help it. The scorer rewards precise, natural academic words — 'significant', 'contribute', 'whereas' — used correctly, not a memorised word salad.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: How are spelling errors treated in the essay?
o: Each misspelt word loses marks under the spelling/form traits
questions.e: Spelling is scored: every misspelt word costs. There is no autocorrect and no spellcheck in the test interface. Your 3-minute check must include a spelling pass — especially doubled letters, -ie/-ei, and plural forms.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: Which sentence shows correct complex grammar for a high score?
o: 'Although governments invest heavily, rural schools still lack resources, which widens inequality.'
'Schools lack resources. Governments invest. Inequality widens.'
'The reason is because of the fact that...'
questions.e: Option A shows subordination ('Although...'), relative clause ('which...') and precise vocabulary — the grammatical range scorers reward. B is correct but too simple for top bands; C is wordy ('the reason is because'); D has a pronoun-doubling error.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: You have no ideas for the prompt. What should you do?
o: Write about a different topic you know
Use the 3-minute plan: take ANY clear position and invent plausible examples — ideas are not fact-checked
questions.e: Essays are not fact-checked: a clear position with plausible invented examples ('a 2023 school survey found...') scores fully. Off-topic writing scores near zero for content; blank scores zero everything. Always take a side — even a boring one argued well beats brilliance with no position.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: What is 'task achievement' in the PTE essay?
o: Fully answering the prompt: position + developed ideas + relevant examples + conclusion
questions.e: Task achievement = do what was asked: address all parts of the prompt, state a position, develop it, conclude. A fluent 250-word essay that ignores half the prompt fails content. Read the prompt twice in planning and check each clause is answered.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: Which conclusion is effective?
o: 'In conclusion, for the reasons discussed, the benefits of online learning outweigh its drawbacks.'
No conclusion — the body says it all
'In conclusion, I will now summarise my summary.'
questions.e: Restate the position crisply without new arguments — that is all a conclusion must do. Apologetic or meta conclusions ('that's all I know') damage the final impression; no conclusion leaves task achievement incomplete.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: How do you avoid the word-count zero in the essay?
o: Target 230–260 and glance at the on-screen counter before submitting
questions.e: The screen shows a live word count: target 230–260 (safe margins both sides) and verify before submitting. Under 120 or over 380 = zero. Hand-counting wastes minutes; the counter is authoritative.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: Which is better: simple correct sentences or complex error-filled ones?
o: Simple and correct beats complex and wrong; best is complex AND correct
questions.e: Accuracy first, then range: error-filled complexity loses more grammar marks than it gains in range. Build from a base of correct simple sentences, then add one subordinate clause per sentence once you can do it cleanly. The top band is complex + correct.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: What should the introduction NOT contain?
questions.e: Examples belong in body paragraphs — front-loading them in the intro wastes the position statement's punch and unbalances the essay. Intro = paraphrase + thesis (+ optional roadmap). Save evidence for the body.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: A prompt asks: 'Some say X, others say Y. Discuss both views and give your opinion.' You only discuss X. Result?
o: Task achievement failure — both views AND your opinion are required
questions.e: Multi-part prompts are checklists: discuss X, discuss Y, give YOUR opinion. Missing a part caps content/task-achievement regardless of beautiful writing. In planning, tick each clause of the prompt and assign it a paragraph.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: Which practice routine builds essay skill fastest?
o: Write 2–3 timed essays weekly with the 3-14-3 method, then self-check against a trait checklist
questions.e: Timed writing + trait checklist (position? 2 developed body paras? 230–260 words? linkers? spelling pass?) builds the actual exam skill. Reading models without writing is passive; templates produce generic content the scoring now punishes.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: What is the 'fence-sitting' error?
o: Sitting too long on one idea
Refusing to take a clear position ('both sides have points' with no verdict)
questions.e: Fence-sitting = no clear thesis. Scorers reward a developed position; 'both sides have merit' with no verdict reads as task avoidance. You may acknowledge the other side — then state clearly which side wins and why.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: Which sentence has a subject-verb agreement error?
questions.e: 'The number... has' — 'number' is singular (contrast 'a number of schools have', where 'a number of' = plural). This is the classic agreement trap. 'Data' as plural ('data show') is accepted in academic style; 'each... has' is correct.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: Why is copying the prompt verbatim in the intro risky?
o: Excessive copying is flagged; paraphrase to show vocabulary range
questions.e: Lifting whole prompt sentences shows zero vocabulary range and can trigger copied-text penalties. Paraphrase: swap synonyms, change structures ('Some argue that...' → 'It is often claimed that...'). A few shared key terms are fine; whole clauses are not.

questions.subject: Write Essay
questions.q: Your essay is at 190 words with 2 minutes left. Best move?
o: Add one more developed sentence to a body paragraph (example or explanation) to clear 200
questions.e: Under 200 risks thin content (and under 120 = zero). One more genuine sentence — an example, a consequence — adds real content and crosses 200 safely. Repetition and filler adjectives add words but no content; both are detectable.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: Reading & Writing: Fill in the Blanks (drag and drop) gives you a text with 5–6 gaps. What decides each answer?
o: Grammar (collocations, word forms) + meaning in context — test each option IN the sentence
questions.e: R&W FIB tests grammar + vocabulary in context: insert each candidate into the gap and read the whole sentence — the right word fits grammatically AND logically. Length and position are irrelevant. Since 2025 these items are Reading-only (the Writing donation ended).

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'The committee ___ the proposal after hours of debate.' Options: approved / approval / approving / approve. Answer?
questions.e: 'The committee ___ the proposal' needs a past-tense main verb: 'approved'. 'Approval' is a noun, 'approving' needs a helper verb, 'approve' is present. Identify what the gap NEEDS (verb? noun? adjective?) before looking at options — need-first beats option-first.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: '___ the rain, the match continued.' Options: Despite / Because / Although / During. Answer?
questions.e: '___ the rain' needs a preposition + noun phrase: 'Despite the rain'. 'Although' needs a clause ('although it rained'); 'because' reverses the logic; 'during the rain' is grammatical but the contrast meaning demands 'despite'. Preposition-vs-conjunction is the #1 FIB grammar test.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: What is a 'collocation' and why does it matter in FIB?
o: Words that naturally pair (make a decision, take responsibility) — the expected pairing is often the answer
questions.e: Collocations = natural word partnerships: you 'make' a decision (not 'do'), 'take' responsibility (not 'give'). FIB options often include a grammatically fine but unidiomatic pairing — the collocating word is the key. Build a collocation notebook from every practice text.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'She has worked here ___ 2019.' Options: for / since / from / at. Answer?
questions.e: 'Since 2019' — since + starting point; for + duration ('for five years'). 'From 2019' needs a 'to/until'; 'at 2019' is wrong. Since/for is a permanent FIB favourite — point in time = since, length of time = for.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'The results were ___ surprising.' Options: much / very / more / most. Answer?
questions.e: 'Very surprising' — very + adjective. 'Much' modifies comparatives/verbs ('much improved'), not plain adjectives. This adverb-placement pattern recurs constantly: very + adjective, much + comparative.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: How many Reorder Paragraph items appear, and what is the method?
o: 2–3; find the topic sentence (standalone, general), then chain pronoun/logical links
questions.e: 2–3 Reorder items: first find the independent topic sentence (general, no pronouns pointing backwards), then link chains — pronouns refer to earlier nouns, time markers sequence events, 'however/therefore' signal relationships. Never start with a sentence containing 'this/these/he/they' unresolved.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: Reorder: which sentence is most likely FIRST? A) 'He later became president.' B) 'These policies transformed the economy.' C) 'Roosevelt took office in 1933 during the Great Depression.' D) 'However, critics disagreed.'
questions.e: C is the standalone general opener: named subject, no backward pronouns, sets time/context. A ('He') and B ('These policies') need antecedents; D ('However') needs a previous claim. The first sentence introduces; it never refers back.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: In Reorder Paragraphs, what does 'this discovery' in a sentence tell you?
o: It must come AFTER the sentence naming the discovery
questions.e: Demonstratives (this/that/these/those) + noun = anaphoric reference: the discovery must be named in an earlier sentence. Chain them: find the naming sentence, place the 'this X' sentence after it. Unresolved demonstratives are the best placement clues in the task.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: Reading: Multiple Choice (Multiple Answers) — what is the scoring trap?
o: -1 for each wrong option: only select options you can justify from the text
questions.e: MCQ-MA uses negative marking: +1 per correct option, −1 per wrong one. Selecting all five 'to be safe' can net zero or negative. Rule: select only options with direct text evidence; when unsure between 2 and 3 options, take the 2 you can prove.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: Reading MCQ Single Answer: the BEST approach is:
o: Read the question first, then scan for the answer — options often quote the text with one word changed
questions.e: Question-first scanning: the options are text-based, and distractors typically echo passage wording with a fatal twist (a changed qualifier, reversed cause-effect). Reading the passage cold wastes your 29 minutes; general knowledge is never the key.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'The new policy aims to reduce carbon ___.' Options: emission / emissions / emit / emitting. Answer?
questions.e: 'Carbon emissions' — the standard collocation is plural. 'Carbon emission' (singular) is unidiomatic; 'emit/emitting' are verb forms that cannot follow 'carbon' here. When a technical collocation exists, it overrides generic grammar guessing.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'Neither of the solutions ___ perfect.' Options: are / is / were / be. Answer?
questions.e: 'Neither of... is' — neither/either/none + of-phrase takes singular verb in formal English. 'Were' is past (the sentence is present); 'are' is the plural trap. Neither/either/none = singular is a tested rule — memorise it.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'The manager, ___ team won the award, resigned.' Options: whose / who's / which / that. Answer?
questions.e: 'Whose team' = possessive relative. 'Who's' = 'who is' (nonsense here); 'which/that team won' breaks the clause structure. Whose/who's is a permanent FIB distractor pair — expand the contraction mentally to check.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: What is the single highest-value Reading task type?
o: R&W Fill in the Blanks (5–6 items, 2 points each)
questions.e: R&W FIB: 5–6 items × 2 points = 10–12 Reading marks — the densest Reading source, especially after 2025 made it Reading-only. Many 79-target plans treat FIB as the entire Reading strategy: master collocations and grammar, and Reading takes care of itself.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: Reading FIB (drag & drop, 4–5 items): how does it differ from R&W FIB?
o: Word bank is shared across gaps — each word used once; grammar matters less, meaning more
questions.e: Reading FIB gives one bank for all gaps (each word used once) and leans on vocabulary-in-context over grammar. Strategy: fill the certain gaps first, shrinking the bank — process of elimination is legitimate here since options are finite and exclusive.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: '___ his illness, he attended the meeting.' Options: Despite / Although / Because of / In spite. Answer?
questions.e: 'Despite his illness' — despite + noun phrase. 'Although' needs a clause ('although he was ill'); 'because of' reverses logic; 'in spite' is incomplete without 'of' ('in spite of'). 'In spite of' would also be correct — the bank gives only one right answer, so check completions.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'The experiment was ___ in 2020.' Options: conducted / conduct / conducting / conduction. Answer?
questions.e: 'Was conducted' — passive needs past participle. 'Was conduct' is ungrammatical; 'was conducting' is active-continuous (wrong meaning); 'conduction' is a noun. 'Be + past participle' = passive is the most tested verb pattern in FIB.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: How should you manage the 29–30 Reading minutes?
o: Front-load R&W FIB (highest value), then Reading FIB, Reorder; ration MCQ time strictly
Spend 20 minutes on the first text
questions.e: Value-order: R&W FIB first (2 marks each), Reading FIB, Reorder, then MCQs with a hard per-item cap — MCQ-MA's negative marking makes overtime there doubly expensive. There are no per-item timers, so discipline is yours alone.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'She is responsible ___ the budget.' Options: for / of / to / with. Answer?
questions.e: 'Responsible for' — fixed preposition collocation. Preposition-after-adjective ('responsible for', 'aware of', 'interested in', 'good at') is pure memorisation; no logic derives it. Keep a preposition-collocation list.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'The ___ of the new law was immediate.' Options: affect / effect / effective / effectively. Answer?
questions.e: 'The effect... was' — noun needed as subject; effect = noun, affect = verb. Article 'the' + gap + 'was' = noun slot. Affect/effect is the classic FIB noun/verb pair — let the surrounding grammar name the word class first.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: Reorder trap: two sentences both look like openers. You should:
o: Choose the more GENERAL one (no names, dates, pronouns); the specific one follows
questions.e: Generality decides: the opener is the broadest statement ('Economic reforms changed Asia'); specifics ('In 1991, India devalued the rupee') follow. Dates, names and numbers usually belong to supporting sentences, not the topic sentence.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'He denied ___ the money.' Options: to take / taking / take / taken. Answer?
questions.e: 'Denied taking' — deny + gerund. Verb-pattern memorisation: deny/admit/enjoy/finish/mind + -ing; want/decide/agree + to-infinitive. These patterns are closed sets — learn the lists and FIB gerund items become free marks.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'There ___ been many changes.' Options: has / have / is / are. Answer?
questions.e: 'There have been' — existential 'there' agrees with the following noun ('changes' = plural). 'There is/are' follows the same rule. The trap is treating 'there' as the subject — the real subject comes after the verb.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: What does 'reading for the gap, not the text' mean?
o: Let the 5–6 words around the gap (grammar + logic) decide before re-reading broadly
questions.e: FIB is won in the immediate neighbourhood: the words before/after the gap determine the word class, collocation and logic. Master the 10-word window first; only zoom out when the local clues are ambiguous. Global re-reading is the time sink to avoid.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'The two companies decided to ___ forces.' Options: join / unite / combine / merge. Then: 'join forces' is the collocation — but which is scored?
questions.e: 'Join forces' is the fixed idiom — the others are grammatical but unidiomatic here. This is the purest collocation test: grammar cannot separate the options, only idiom knowledge can. Read widely; collocations are caught, not taught.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: MCQ-MA: you are sure of 2 options and torn on a 3rd. You should:
o: Select only the 2 certain ones — a wrong pick costs a mark
questions.e: Negative marking math: a certain +1 each for two options vs a gamble risking −1. Expected value of guessing the 3rd at 50% confidence is zero — and wrong answers also signal misunderstanding. Bank the certain, skip the doubtful.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: '___ 2020, the company ___ grown rapidly.' Options for gap 1: Since / For; gap 2: has / have. Answers?
questions.e: 'Since 2020' (point in time) + 'the company has grown' (singular subject). Two rules in one item — FIB loves stacking since/for with subject-verb agreement. Solve gaps left to right, letting each answer constrain the next.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: Which Reading task should you NEVER leave blank?
o: R&W FIB and Reorder — no negative marking, so attempt every gap
questions.e: FIB and Reorder have no negative marking: a guessed gap can only help. MCQ-MA is the exception — wrong options subtract. Rule of thumb: attempt everything except uncertain MCQ-MA options.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'The theory was first ___ in the 19th century.' Options: proposed / proposal / proposing / propose. Answer?
questions.e: 'Was proposed' — passive past participle again ('be + V3'). FIB recycles a small set of grammar patterns: passive, gerund/infinitive, subject-verb agreement, articles, prepositions. Master the pattern list and half the items solve themselves.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'A ___ number of students failed.' Options: large / big / huge / vast. Which fits the academic collocation?
