questions.e: 'A large number of' is the fixed academic collocation — 'big number' and 'huge number' sound informal/wrong to the key. Register matters in FIB: academic texts demand academic pairings. When two options seem synonymous, pick the formal one.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: Reorder: the paragraph includes 'First,...', 'Next,...', 'Finally,...'. You should:
o: Ignore them — sequence words are decorative
Use them as a skeleton: order the sequenced sentences, then fit the rest around them
Treat each as a separate paragraph
questions.e: Sequence markers are free ordering: First → Next → Finally gives you three locked positions; the remaining sentences slot between them via pronoun/logic links. Test-makers include them deliberately — using them is not cheating, it is reading.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'He is the ___ experienced member.' Options: most / more / much / many. Answer?
questions.e: 'The most experienced' — superlative with 'the'. 'More' needs a comparison ('more experienced than'); 'much/many' cannot modify the adjective directly. The + superlative vs comparative + than is a closed, testable rule.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: What is 'textual evidence discipline' in Reading MCQs?
o: Every selected option must point to specific supporting words in the passage
questions.e: Evidence discipline: for each option, find the passage words that prove or kill it. 'Sounds true' options are engineered distractors — they are true in real life but unsupported by the text. The key follows the text, never the world.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: '___ you need help, ask me.' Options: Should / If / Unless / Were. Which TWO are grammatical, and which is the better key?
o: Should — formal inversion ('Should you need help') beats plain 'If' in academic texts
questions.e: Both 'Should you need help' (inversion) and 'If you need help' are grammatical — but the gap precedes 'you need', so 'Should you need' fits the slot while 'If' would need 'If you need'. Formal inversion (Should/Were/Had + subject) is a favourite FIB structure: recognise the pattern, don't fear it.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'The museum houses artefacts ___ back centuries.' Options: dating / dated / date / dates. Answer?
questions.e: 'Artefacts dating back centuries' — reduced relative clause ('which date back' → 'dating back'). 'Dated' would mean the artefacts were assigned a date (wrong meaning); 'date/dates' break the clause. Reduced relatives (-ing/-ed phrases) are advanced FIB staples.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: You consistently finish Reading with 5 minutes unused. You should:
o: Reinvest in R&W FIB: re-test each gap by inserting your choice and reading the sentence aloud in your head
questions.e: Spare Reading minutes belong to R&W FIB review: re-insert each chosen word and re-read the sentence — second-pass reading catches logic slips the first pass missed. MCQs are lower value per minute; submitting early donates marks.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'Not only ___ the policy unpopular, but it was costly.' Options: was / were / is / be. Answer?
questions.e: 'Not only was the policy...' — negative-fronting triggers inversion (verb before subject), past tense matching 'was costly'. Fronted negatives (Not only, Never, Rarely, Seldom) + inversion is a high-level FIB pattern: spot the fronting, invert the verb.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: Which statement about Reading preparation is TRUE?
o: Daily FIB practice (20 items) + collocation notebook + timed Reorder sets beats passive reading
questions.e: Reading is a skills test, not a knowledge test: daily deliberate FIB reps build the grammar-collocation reflex, and timed Reorder sets build linking speed. Novels help vocabulary slowly but do not train gap-solving; speed-reading tricks collapse on FIB logic.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'The findings, ___ were published yesterday, caused a stir.' Options: which / that / who / whose. Answer?
questions.e: '...findings, which were published...' — non-defining clause set off by commas takes 'which', never 'that'. Comma + gap + clause = non-defining: which (things) / who (people). 'That' after a comma is always wrong — a free mark if you spot the commas.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: R&W FIB: 'He ran ___ the hill.' Options: up / to / at / on. The point being tested?
o: Prepositions of movement vs position — 'up the hill' (movement) vs 'on the hill' (position)
questions.e: 'Up the hill' = movement/direction; 'on the hill' = position. FIB preposition items test meaning, not just idiom: picture the scene — running describes motion, so the directional 'up' fits. Visualising the action resolves most preposition gaps.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q: Final check: R&W FIB: '___ the evidence, the jury acquitted him.' Options: In light of / In spite of / Because / Despite. Two fit grammatically — which is the key and why?
o: In light of — acquittal follows FROM evidence (logic), not against it
In spite of — contrast is always the answer
questions.e: 'In light of the evidence' = the evidence explains the acquittal (cause). 'In spite of/Despite' would mean acquitted AGAINST the evidence — illogical. When two options fit grammatically, logic decides: does the sentence's meaning flow with or against the phrase? Acquittal flows WITH evidence.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: Summarize Spoken Text: you hear a 60–90 second lecture ONCE, then get 10 minutes. Your response must be:
questions.e: SST = 50–70 words, full sentences, 10 minutes. One sentence is SWT; 200–300 is the essay. SST feeds Listening AND Writing — it is the highest-value listening task, worth the full 10-minute investment.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: What is the proven SST note-taking method?
o: Keywords + arrows: nouns, numbers, cause→effect, roughly one line per 15 seconds
Write your summary during the audio
questions.e: Keyword triggers with relationship arrows — you cannot transcribe 90 seconds of speech, and writing sentences during the audio splits attention. One line per 15 seconds gives ~6 lines: enough for a 50–70-word summary without drowning.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: SST: the lecture is fast and technical. You catch ~50%. You should:
o: Write 50–70 words from what you caught, in grammatical sentences — partial content still scores
questions.e: SST scoring is proportional: real content words earn marks, invented ones earn nothing (and risk relevance penalties). 50–70 genuine words from half-understanding beats 20 words or fabrication. Never leave an SST blank — it is 10 minutes of double-skill marks.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: SST word count: what happens at 49 or 71 words?
o: Form penalty: the 50–70 window is scored, so count before submitting
questions.e: The 50–70 window is part of Form scoring — outside it you lose form marks (not an automatic zero, unlike SWT's harder edges). The on-screen counter is live: trim or pad to land inside before submitting. Aim 55–65 for safety.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: Which SST summary structure works best?
o: Topic sentence (what the lecture was about) + 3–4 key points as full sentences
questions.e: Topic sentence + developed points in proper sentences: it satisfies Content (key ideas), Grammar (sentence structure) and Vocabulary simultaneously. Keyword salad fails grammar; a single 70-word sentence risks run-on errors.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: SST feeds which two skills?
questions.e: SST = Listening + Writing: you must comprehend the lecture (Listening) and render it in grammatical written English (Writing). Weak spellers and grammarians lose Writing marks here — proofread your SST like a mini-essay.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: How many SST items appear?
questions.e: Only 1–2 SST items — but each is 10 minutes feeding two skills, making SST the most time-expensive listening task. Quality over quantity: one polished 60-word summary outscores two rushed ones (which you will never have time for).

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: Listening MCQ Multiple Answers: the scoring rule is:
o: +1 correct, −1 wrong — select only options with clear audio evidence
All correct answers must be selected for any mark
questions.e: Same negative marking as Reading MCQ-MA: +1 per correct, −1 per wrong. In listening the evidence is a heard phrase — only select options you can tie to something the speaker actually said. Uncertain options stay unselected.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: Listening MCQ Single Answer: best technique?
o: Read question + options BEFORE the audio plays, then listen for the answer
questions.e: You get time before the audio: read the question and options first so your ears know what to catch. Listening blind then reading means replaying the audio in memory — impossible, since it plays once. Previewing turns listening into targeted catching.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: Highlight Correct Summary: you hear a recording, then choose the paragraph that best summarises it. It feeds:
questions.e: HCS is cross-scored to Listening + Reading — you comprehend by ear, then discriminate summaries by eye. The wrong options are near-misses: one changed detail, one exaggerated claim. Match each summary sentence against what you heard.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: HCS: the best elimination method is:
o: Kill options containing details NEVER mentioned, then choose among survivors
questions.e: Wrong summaries smuggle in unmentioned details or twist one fact — scan each option for a claim the audio never made and eliminate it. Length and position are irrelevant; 'interesting' is not a scoring trait.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: In Listening MCQs, why are options dangerous?
o: Distractors reuse the audio's exact words with twisted meaning — word-matching without understanding fails
questions.e: The classic listening trap: an option quotes the speaker verbatim but reverses the logic ('X causes Y' vs audio's 'Y causes X'). Ears must track MEANING, not vocabulary overlap. Preview-then-listen-for-logic beats word-spotting.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: SST: which notes are USELESS?
o: Full sentences like 'The professor talked about the interesting topic of climate change in great detail'
questions.e: Meta-commentary notes ('the professor talked about...') contain zero content — they summarise the act of lecturing, not the lecture. Notes must be content triggers: nouns, numbers, relationships. If a note could describe ANY lecture, it is useless.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: How should you use the 10 SST minutes?
o: ~1 min organising notes, ~7 min writing 55–65 words, ~2 min checking count/grammar/spelling
questions.e: 1-7-2: organise triggers into 3–4 points, draft 55–65 words, then verify (word count in 50–70? full sentences? verbs agree? key terms spelt right?). Non-stop writing skips the check where easy marks hide; early submit wastes the highest-value listening minutes.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: SST: the lecture's main topic appears in the first 15 seconds. Why does this matter?
o: Your topic sentence is then secured early — even if the rest blurs, the summary has an anchor
questions.e: Lectures front-load the topic: catching the opening secures your summary's first sentence and orients every later note. Even a partial summary with a correct topic sentence earns content marks — the anchor turns fragments into a coherent answer.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: Which spelling habit matters MOST for SST and WFD?
o: Correct spelling of key content words — each misspelt word loses its mark
questions.e: Content words carry the marks: misspell 'photosynthesis' and you lose that word's credit in WFD/SST. Variant consistency (organize vs organise) is accepted. Drill the spelling of 200 high-frequency academic words — it pays in three tasks.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: Listening MCQ: the speaker says 'Most economists agree that...' The question asks what economists agree on. A distractor says 'All economists prove that...' Why is it wrong?
o: It changes the qualifier (most→all) and the verb (agree→prove) — two twists
questions.e: Distractors twist qualifiers (most/all/some), verbs (agree/prove/suggest) and scope. Train your ear on hedging language — 'most', 'tends to', 'suggests' — because the key almost always preserves the speaker's exact level of certainty.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: What is 'predictive listening' in SST?
o: Using the topic to anticipate likely points (causes, effects, examples) so your ears catch them
questions.e: Before/during the audio, prime expectations: a lecture on 'urban traffic' will cover causes, effects, solutions. Primed ears catch predicted vocabulary faster and note-taking becomes slotting ideas into expected buckets — not magic, just schema activation.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: SST: your draft is 45 words. Best fix?
o: Add one more genuine key point as a sentence to enter the 50–70 window
questions.e: 45 words = form penalty zone. One more real point (an example, a consequence from your notes) adds content AND fixes form. Synonym-repetition and filler add words but no content — padding without substance is detectable and unrewarded.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: Which is worth more per minute: SST or MCQ-SA?
o: SST — 10 minutes feeding two skills with proportional content credit
questions.e: SST dominates: 10 minutes, two skills, partial credit for every genuine content word. An MCQ-SA is one mark for one skill. If listening time runs short, protect SST absolutely — steal minutes from MCQs, never from SST or WFD.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: Final SST check: which summary would score highest? Lecture on bees declining from pesticides, habitat loss, disease; solutions: flower strips, reduced spraying.
o: 'Bees are important insects that live in hives and make honey.'
'The lecture discussed declining bee populations, attributing it to pesticides, habitat loss and disease, and proposed flower strips and reduced spraying as solutions.'
'Pesticides pesticides habitat disease bees decline solution flowers.'
'I think we should save the bees because they are nice.'
questions.e: Option B: topic + three causes + two solutions in grammatical sentences — the SST formula. In the real task you would expand it with one detail per point to reach 50–70 words. A is off-topic trivia, C is keyword salad (grammar zero), D is opinion (content zero). Coverage + structure first, then tune length with genuine details.

questions.subject: Listening: SST & MCQs
questions.q: The 2026 test-taker's biggest SST mistake is:
o: Treating it as dictation: trying to transcribe instead of summarising key points
questions.e: Transcription attempts collapse around second 30 — you fall behind, panic, and produce fragments. SST rewards selection: 5–6 trigger-lines → 55–65 words of summary. Summarise, don't transcribe; the audio plays once and waits for no one.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Listening: Fill in the Blanks — you hear a recording while reading a transcript with gaps, typing the missing words. Key technique?
o: Type what you EXPECT before listening
Track the transcript with your cursor/eyes and type the word the moment you hear it
questions.e: Follow-and-catch: keep your eyes on the text slightly ahead of the audio and type each missing word as it sounds. Predicting or memorising fails because the gaps are content words you cannot guess; typing after fails because you will forget the exact forms. Since 2025 these items are Listening-only.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Listening FIB: the speaker says 'photosynthesis'. You type 'fotosynthesis'. Result?
o: Wrong — exact spelling required; only that word's mark is lost
questions.e: Listening FIB is word-by-word: exact spelling or no mark for that gap. Phonetic approximations fail. But one misspelt gap does not kill the item — every other correct gap still scores. This is why the 200-word academic spelling list matters.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: How many Listening FIB items appear?
questions.e: 2–3 Listening FIB items — few, but each gap is a Listening mark and the task is highly trainable. Combined with WFD they make spelling the most leveraged micro-skill in the Listening part.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Listening FIB: you missed a gap mid-recording. You should:
o: Leave it and keep following — one gap lost beats losing the thread and missing five
questions.e: Keep moving: the audio never pauses, and dwelling on a lost gap guarantees missing the next ones. A blank gap costs one mark; losing the thread costs the item. Note-takers call this the 'sacrifice one to save five' rule. (No rewinds exist in PTE.)

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Which words are most often the gaps in Listening FIB?
o: Content words: nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs
questions.e: Gaps target meaning-carriers — nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs. Articles and conjunctions are rarely gapped because they carry no distinctive sound. Train your ear on stressed content words; they are both the gaps and the memory anchors.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Select Missing Word: you hear a recording whose final word/phrase is replaced by a beep, then choose the ending. Best method?
o: Pick the option with the hardest word
Follow the speaker's logic and intonation — the beep completes a thought the context predicts
questions.e: SMW tests prediction: the sentence's logic and the speaker's intonation contour point to the missing ending. Listen for the argument's direction (contrast? conclusion? example?) — the beep is the punchline the whole sentence was building toward.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: SMW: '...and therefore the most logical conclusion is— [beep]'. Options: A) 'that the theory is incorrect.' B) 'bananas.' C) 'that further research is needed, although the theory remains unproven.' D) 'purple.' What works?
o: C — it completes the logical move with the right register; A contradicts 'logical conclusion' framing, B/D are nonsense
questions.e: SMW options include absurd distractors (B, D) to punish random clicking and near-miss logic options (A). The key completes the sentence's rhetorical move: a hedged academic conclusion after 'the most logical conclusion is'. Match logic + register, and absurd options eliminate themselves.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: How many Select Missing Word items appear, and what do they feed?
questions.e: Just 1–2 SMW items feeding Listening — low volume, moderate value. Do not over-invest preparation here; the beep-completion skill transfers from general listening practice. Protect SST, FIB and WFD time first.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Listening FIB: the transcript shows 'The results were ___ published in Nature.' You hear 'eventually'. You type 'eventualy'. This tests:
o: Spelling under time pressure — double letters and suffixes (-ally, -ence, -tion) are the classic failure points
questions.e: You HEARD it right and still lost the mark — the classic Listening FIB failure is spelling, not hearing. High-risk patterns: doubled consonants (eventually, occurred), -ally vs -aly, -ence/-ance, -tion/-sion. A spelling drill list of these patterns is the highest-ROI listening prep after WFD itself.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: What is 'shadowing' and how does it help Listening FIB?
o: Repeating audio with a 1-second delay while listening — it trains ear-to-hand speed for catching and typing words
questions.e: Shadowing (speak along just behind the speaker) wires the listen→produce pipeline at speed — exactly what follow-and-catch typing demands. It also attunes your ear to connected speech ('gonna', 'wanna', reduced vowels) so fewer words blur past unrecognised.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Listening FIB: the speaker has a strong unfamiliar accent. Best coping strategy?
o: Read ahead in the transcript — grammar and context narrow each gap to a few possible words, so partial hearing suffices
questions.e: The transcript is your lifeline: 'The ___ was invented in 1876 by Alexander Graham Bell' needs almost no hearing ('telephone' is forced by context). Read 5–6 words ahead of the audio; context + fragments of sound solve most gaps even through a thick accent.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Which preparation helps Listening FIB most?
o: Dictation practice: listen to 60-second clips and transcribe them fully, then check spelling
questions.e: Full-transcription dictation is FIB in its purest form: catch every word, spell every word, check against the transcript. Subtitled movies let your eyes do the work your ears must do in the test. 15 minutes of daily dictation transforms FIB scores in weeks.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: SMW: the speaker lists problems and says 'The only viable solution, therefore, is— [beep]'. The key will be:
o: A solution consistent with the problems listed
questions.e: 'The only viable solution' + 'therefore' = the beep resolves the listed problems. SMW keys always complete the discourse function the sentence announces (solution, contrast, conclusion, example). Track the function words — therefore, however, for example — they are signposts to the beep.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: True or False: in Listening FIB you can edit your typed words after the audio ends.
o: True — you get a short window before the item advances; use it to fix spelling
questions.e: You get a brief review window after the audio: use it ONLY for spelling fixes on words you caught, not for agonising over missed gaps (you cannot replay). A 10-second spelling pass rescues marks — 'recieve' → 'receive' is a free mark.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Listening FIB: '...a ___ of 3.2 percent...' You hear something like 'growth/rose'. The transcript grammar says the gap precedes 'of 3.2 percent'. The word is:
o: growth — 'a growth of 3.2 percent' (noun forced by 'a ___ of')
questions.e: 'A ___ of' forces a noun: 'growth'. 'Rose' is a verb, 'growing' a participle, 'grow' a base verb — none fit the article+noun frame. Grammar-first gap solving: let the frame ('a ___ of') name the word class before your ears confirm the word.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Which note-taking is allowed during Listening FIB?
o: None needed — you type directly into the gaps; the board is for SST/WFD
questions.e: FIB needs no noteboard: your output goes straight into the on-screen gaps. Save the erasable booklet for SST (trigger notes) and WFD (first-letter jots). Fumbling with the board during FIB splits attention from the follow-and-catch task.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: The beep in SMW replaces:
o: Only the final word or short phrase
questions.e: SMW beeps only the tail — the final word(s). Everything before it is intact context engineered to make the ending predictable. If you understood the sentence's direction, the beep is nearly redundant; if you zoned out, no option will save you.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Listening FIB: you consistently type the word but misspell suffixes (-ant/-ent, -able/-ible). The fix?
o: A targeted suffix drill: 50 words each of -ant/-ent, -able/-ible, -tion/-sion with sentence dictation
questions.e: Suffix confusion is systematic, not random — so drill it systematically: word lists in minimal pairs (dependent/dependant, credible/creditable... ) via dictation until the patterns are automatic. Speed never fixes a knowledge gap; skipping donates marks.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: What distinguishes Highlight Correct Summary from Select Missing Word?
o: HCS: hear full recording, pick the best written summary (Listening+Reading). SMW: hear recording with beeped ending, pick the completion (Listening).
questions.e: HCS = whole-recording comprehension + summary discrimination (cross-scored Listening+Reading); SMW = ending prediction (Listening). HCS gives you the full content — the challenge is the near-miss options. SMW withholds the ending — the challenge is prediction.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Best daily listening routine for the FIB/SMW/HCS cluster?
o: 30 min active: 10 min dictation/transcription + 10 min beep-prediction clips + 10 min summary-matching
questions.e: Active beats passive: transcription trains FIB catch-and-spell, beep-prediction clips train SMW logic, summary-matching trains HCS discrimination. Background podcasts feel productive but test nothing — the exam never lets you zone out, so practice shouldn't either.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Listening FIB: the gap is '___ research shows...' and you hear 'recent'. Why is hearing the FIRST sound critical?
o: Initial consonants disambiguate most words ('recent' vs 'decent'); endings blur in connected speech
The scorer only checks first letters
questions.e: In natural speech, word endings reduce and blur ('recent studies' → 'recen' + 'studies') while onsets stay crisp. Training your ear on initial sounds + stress patterns identifies words even when endings wash out. 'Decent research' vs 'recent research' is decided at the first phoneme.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: SMW: which option type is ALMOST NEVER the key?
o: The absurd/unrelated option — it exists to catch random clickers
The option echoing the speaker's vocabulary
questions.e: Absurd options ('bananas', 'purple') are pure distractor furniture — eliminating them first turns a 4-option guess into a 3-option reasoning task. After elimination, choose by logic + register fit, not by which option 'sounds smart'.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: You have 5 minutes left in Listening with WFD items remaining. You should:
o: Protect WFD absolutely — steal time from any remaining MCQ, never from WFD
questions.e: WFD is the highest-value task in the entire test (3–4 items × word-by-word × two skills). Five rushed minutes on MCQs cannot match one careful WFD item. Triage rule: WFD > SST > FIB > HCS > MCQs, always.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Listening FIB: 'The ___ of the project...' You hear 'scale/scope'. Both fit! How to decide?
o: Replay the initial sound in memory: 'scale' (sk-) vs 'scope' (sk-) — identical onsets! Use the vowel: scale=/eɪ/, scope=/əʊ/. Train vowel discrimination.
questions.e: When onsets match, vowels decide: scale has the 'ay' vowel, scope the 'oh' vowel. This is advanced ear training — minimal-pair drills (scale/scope, ship/sheep, full/fool) build the vowel discrimination that resolves FIB ties. Random guessing here is 50/50; trained ears make it 95/5.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Which statement about the Listening part's audio is TRUE?
o: Each recording plays ONCE, with varied accents — there are no replays
questions.e: Once-only playback with international accents is the defining constraint of PTE Listening. Every technique in this chapter (follow-and-catch, preview-then-listen, sacrifice-one-to-save-five) exists because there is no second hearing. Practise with single-play audio only.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: HCS: two summaries differ only in that one says 'the decline began in 1990' and the other 'the decline began in 1980'. You didn't catch the date. You should:
o: Eliminate the other two options first, then pick the date you half-remember — and note dates as a listening target henceforth
questions.e: HCS is single-answer with no negative marking: eliminate the clearly-wrong summaries, then commit to your best memory of the detail. And log the miss — numbers/dates are deliberate HCS discriminators, so train number-catching (years, percentages, quantities) as a micro-skill.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: The common thread of FIB, SMW and HCS preparation is:
o: Single-play active listening: catch content words, track logic, predict endings — all under once-only playback
questions.e: All three tasks share the once-only constraint: FIB catches words live, SMW predicts the withheld ending, HCS comprehends-then-discriminates. The master skill is engaged single-play listening — every drill in this chapter serves it, and no template can substitute for it.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Listening FIB: '...was ___ discovered...' You hear 'accidentally'. The spelling trap is:
questions.e: 'Accidentally': double-c... no — double-L ('accidentaLLy') is the trap, plus the -ally ending. High-frequency FIB words with doubled letters: occurred, beginning, accommodation, accidentally, necessary (one c, double s). Drill the doubling list — it is pure mark-rescue.

questions.subject: Listening: FIB, Summary & Missing
questions.q: Final check — Listening FIB: 'The committee will ___ the proposal next week.' You hear 'consider'. Which spelling is correct?
questions.e: 'Consider': one c, one s... precisely c-o-n-s-i-d-e-r — no doubling, 's' not 'c' in the middle. The distractors show the classic error patterns: c/s confusion and false doubling. When sure of the word, write it once, carefully — then move on.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: Highlight Incorrect Words: you hear a recording while reading its transcript; some words DIFFER. Your job?
o: Click each word in the text that differs from what you hear
questions.e: HIW = click the mismatches: the transcript has substituted words ('economic' for 'economical') and you click each one you catch differing from the audio. It feeds Listening + Reading. Clicking is fast — the skill is hearing word-level differences in real time.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: How many HIW items appear?
questions.e: 2–3 HIW items — small but quick marks for trained ears. Each correctly clicked word scores (+1), each wrong click costs (−1): the same negative-marking logic as MCQ-MA. Click only words you are SURE differed.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: HIW scoring: +1 per correct click, −1 per wrong click. Therefore you should:
o: Click only clear mismatches — uncertain clicks have negative expected value
questions.e: Negative marking math again: a 50%-sure click has expected value zero, and wrong clicks also signal poor discrimination. Click the clear substitutions ('rapidly' heard as 'quickly' in text) and leave the maybes alone. Discipline outscores enthusiasm here.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: Which word pairs are typical HIW substitutions?
o: Synonym swaps (big/large), tense changes (go/went), singular/plural (book/books), negatives (can/cannot)
questions.e: HIW substitutions are meaning-close but form-different: synonyms, inflections, number, negation. Train by reading along and flagging ANY deviation — the test wants proof you process every word, not just the gist. 'Can' vs 'cannot' is the cruellest pair: one phoneme decides.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: Write from Dictation: you hear a sentence ONCE (3–9 seconds), then type it exactly. How is it scored?
o: Word by word: each correct word in the correct sequence scores
questions.e: WFD = per-word credit in sequence: a 12-word sentence with 9 words right earns 9/12 of the marks. This partial credit is why you must type EVERYTHING you caught — fragments score. And each item feeds BOTH Listening and Writing.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: How many WFD items appear, and why are they the #1 priority?
o: 3–4; each scored word-by-word across Listening AND Writing — the densest marks in the test
questions.e: 3–4 WFD items, each ~10–14 words, each word a mark in two skills. Missing one WFD sentence can cost 20+ raw marks across Listening+Writing. No other task concentrates this much score in this few minutes — WFD is the backbone of most 79-plans.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: WFD: the sentence is 'The university library holds over two million volumes.' Best capture method?
o: First letters on the noteboard during audio (T U L H O T M V), then expand while typing
questions.e: First-letter jotting keeps pace with speech where full words cannot; expanding immediately after uses fresh echoic memory. Typing purely from memory works for short sentences but degrades past ~10 words. Full transcription during audio makes you miss the ending.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: WFD: you caught 8 of 12 words. You should:
o: Type the 8 words in order with gaps where unsure
Type the 8 words you caught in their correct positions — partial credit for each
Leave it blank — incomplete answers score zero
questions.e: Type what you caught, in order: 8/12 words = 8/12 marks. Blank = 0; invented words = 0 for those slots AND they can break the sequence credit. Partial credit is the test's gift — unwrap it every time.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: WFD: which words are most commonly missed?
o: Short function words (a, the, of, to, and) and plural -s / tense -ed endings
questions.e: Content nouns are the EASY catches — they are stressed. Marks leak on the small stuff: articles, prepositions, plural -s, past -ed, third-person -s. Train your ear on endings: 'book' vs 'books' is one phoneme worth one mark, and WFD sentences are full of them.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: WFD: 'The chemistry building is closed for renovation this semester.' The high-risk words are:
o: is, for, this (function words) and the -ed in 'closed', -tion in 'renovation'
questions.e: The content words (chemistry, building, renovation, semester) announce themselves; the marks die on 'is/for/this' and the endings ('closED', 'renovaTION'). Proofread WFD answers specifically for articles, prepositions and suffixes — that is where 79s are won.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: Should WFD answers include correct punctuation and capitalisation?
o: Capitalise the first word; final full stop optional but harmless — words are what score
questions.e: Only the words score (in sequence). Start with a capital letter as good practice; the final period is accepted but unscored. Do not waste seconds on commas mid-sentence — spend them verifying articles and endings, which ARE scored.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: WFD: the speaker says '...have been widely criticised.' You type '...have been widely criticized.' Result?
o: Wrong — spelling must match the speaker's country
Correct — both British and American spellings are accepted
questions.e: PTE accepts all standard English spelling variants: criticised/criticized, organise/organize, colour/color. Pick ONE variant and stay consistent within an item. Spelling-variant anxiety wastes time — the engine does not care which standard you use.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: How much time do you get to type each WFD sentence?
o: No fixed per-item timer, but the section timer runs — type promptly and move on
questions.e: WFD has no individual countdown, but Listening's 30–43 minutes are shared: dawdling on one sentence steals from the rest. Rhythm: jot first-letters during audio, expand-type immediately, 10-second proofread (articles/endings), next item.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: WFD practice: which drill works?
o: Daily dictation: 15 sentences, first-letter jot → type → check word-by-word, logging error patterns
questions.e: The WFD loop: listen once → jot → type → score per word → log WHAT you missed (articles? endings? spelling?). The error log is the gold: if 70% of misses are plural -s, you drill plural -s. Reading aloud trains the wrong direction (production, not reception).

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: HIW: the text says 'The results were quite surprising.' You hear 'The results were quite surprised.' You should:
o: Click 'surprising' — surprising/surprised is exactly the -ing/-ed substitution type
questions.e: 'Surprising' (thing that surprises) vs 'surprised' (person who is surprised) — the audio's adjective describes the wrong noun, a classic HIW swap. Click the TEXT word that differs from the audio. -ing/-ed adjective swaps are HIW staples: interesting/interested, boring/bored, exciting/excited.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: WFD: you are unsure whether the sentence was '...for the project' or '...of the project'. You should:
o: Type your best guess — a wrong function word loses one mark; a blank loses it too, and guesses are sometimes right
questions.e: Never leave blanks in WFD: a guess has upside (you might be right) and no extra downside (wrong = same zero as blank). Typing both breaks sequence scoring. When torn between two function words, pick the one that fits the verb's collocation ('responsible FOR the project').

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: What is 'echoic memory' and why does WFD depend on it?
o: The 3–4 second auditory trace after hearing — WFD typing must happen inside it before it fades
questions.e: Echoic memory holds raw audio for ~3–4 seconds: this is why you jot DURING the sentence and type IMMEDIATELY after — waiting 20 seconds lets the trace decay into gist ('something about the library'). Speed of capture, not depth of memory, is the WFD skill.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: WFD: which error pattern should you check FIRST in proofreading?
o: Articles (a/the), prepositions, and -s/-ed endings — the highest-frequency misses
questions.e: The 10-second WFD proofread has one job: scan for the small words and endings. Read your typed sentence and ask of each slot: article needed? plural? tense ending? This single habit is worth several raw marks per test — the cheapest marks in PTE.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: HIW: best physical technique?
o: Follow the text with your cursor/eyes word by word, finger ready to click the instant audio and text diverge
questions.e: Synchronised following: eyes on the exact word being spoken, click reflex primed. Reading ahead desyncs you (you will miss the divergence point); eyes-off means no detection at all. HIW is a vigilance task — attention, not knowledge, is tested.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: A student scores 90 in Reading but 55 in Listening. The WFD-centred diagnosis is:
o: Listening is the bottleneck: prioritise WFD + RS + SST (all cross-skill), since Reading is already banked
questions.e: Skills Profile thinking: Reading 90 means comprehension is fine — the gap is auditory processing under once-only playback. WFD, RS and SST all feed Listening while leveraging existing comprehension. More reading cannot fix an ear problem; targeted dictation can.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: WFD: 'Accommodation is provided for all first-year students.' The spelling landmines are:
questions.e: 'Accommodation' is the #1 misspelt WFD word in every learner corpus: ac-COM-mo-da-tion (double c, double m). 'First-year' as a compound adjective takes the hyphen. These are memorisation items — put the top-50 WFD spelling demons on flashcards.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: Which WFD sentence is HARDER to score on, and why? A) 'Cats sleep.' B) 'The government's controversial proposal has been widely debated in parliament.'
o: B — function words (The, has, been, in), endings (controversial, debated), and spelling (government, parliament) multiply the miss chances
questions.e: Difficulty = number of scorable small words and endings, not sentence length alone. B packs articles, auxiliaries, prepositions, suffixes and two spelling demons into 11 words. Train on B-type sentences; A-type sentences are free marks — bank them in seconds.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: True or False: you may replay the WFD sentence if you missed the beginning.
o: False — once-only playback; the beginning must be caught live via first-letter jotting
questions.e: No replays anywhere in PTE Listening. The beginning of the sentence is the most vulnerable (you are still orienting) — which is why jotting starts the instant audio starts, not after you 'understand' it. Catch first, comprehend while typing.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: HIW: you clicked 4 words, 3 correct and 1 wrong. Your score for the item?
questions.e: +1 per correct click, −1 per wrong: 3−1 = 2. This arithmetic is why uncertain clicks are vandalism against your own score. When in doubt, leave it out — a missed mismatch costs 1; a wrong click costs 1 AND cancels a correct one.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: The ultimate WFD warm-up, 5 minutes before the test starts, is:
o: One slow dictation round (a 10-word sentence, jot → type → check) to prime the ear-hand pipeline
questions.e: Prime the pipeline, not the panic: a single easy dictation rep activates echoic capture, first-letter jotting and the proofread scan. Cramming new words now only adds anxiety; the ear-hand loop is what the first WFD item will demand within minutes.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: Which statement BEST captures the WFD master rule?
o: 'Catch everything, in order, spelled right — every word is a mark in two skills, and partial credit rewards every fragment.'
questions.e: The master rule compresses the whole chapter: full capture (jot live), sequence (order matters), spelling (exact), and never blank (partial credit). WFD is not a talent test — it is a procedure, and procedures can be drilled to near-perfection.

questions.subject: HIW & Dictation
questions.q: HIW: the audio says '...cannot be ignored.' The text reads '...can be ignored.' This tests:
o: Negation hearing — the n't phoneme flips meaning entirely; missing it inverts the sentence
questions.e: Can/can't is a one-phoneme distinction carrying total meaning reversal — and it is a deliberate HIW favourite. Train minimal-pair negation hearing (can/can't, will/won't, is/isn't) because the same distinction decides WFD and FIB marks too.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: What must you carry to the test centre?
o: Your original valid passport (name matching registration)
questions.e: Original valid passport, name exactly matching your myPTE booking — non-negotiable. Phones are locked away before the test; photocopies and other IDs are rejected. Check passport validity weeks ahead, not the night before.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: What is the single most important timing rule in PTE?
o: Never leave high-value items (WFD, SST, SWT, Essay) unfinished — protect them first in each part
questions.e: Triage beats perfection: an unfinished WFD or blank essay zeroes the densest marks in the test. The hierarchy — WFD > SST > SWT/Essay > FIB > RS/RA > MCQs — should govern every timing decision. Perfecting a 1-mark MCQ while an SST sits blank is the classic timing failure.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: During the test, your neighbour's loud speaking breaks your concentration. You should:
o: Refocus on your screen; the headset mic is directional and practice with noise inoculates you
questions.e: Noise is a known test condition — centres seat many candidates together. Train with background chatter so exam-day noise is familiar, not shocking. Complaining mid-section wastes YOUR timer; the mic captures your voice, not theirs.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: What should you do in the 10-minute break?
o: Restroom, water, light snack, deep breaths — no phones or study material allowed
questions.e: Break = recovery: water, restroom, stretch, breathe. Phones and notes are prohibited (biometric re-check on return); discussing items with others helps nothing and risks misconduct flags. Return 2 minutes early to resettle.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: Your Score Report shows Listening 52, others 70+. Your retake plan should be:
o: Targeted drill: WFD + SST + RS + Listening FIB daily for 3–4 weeks, then retake
questions.e: Skills-Profile-driven retakes: one weak skill = targeted micro-drills on its highest-value tasks, not general restudy. Listening 52 with Reading 70+ is an ear problem (once-only processing), fixed by dictation-family drills. Immediate blind retakes usually reproduce the same profile.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: How should you use the official Scored Practice Test?
o: After 2–3 weeks of preparation, under strict timed conditions, as a diagnostic dress rehearsal
questions.e: Scored mocks are precious (paid, limited): use them as dress rehearsals once preparation is underway — timed, single sitting, real conditions. Too early wastes the diagnostic (you don't know the format yet); the night before wastes the learning window. One scored mock mid-prep + one near the end is the classic pattern.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: What does 'dress rehearsal' mean in PTE preparation?
o: A full timed mock: 2 hours, one sitting, no pauses, noteboard, headset — simulating test-day pressure
questions.e: Full-simulation mocks build the stamina and timing judgment the real test demands — including the 3-second mic rule, no-replay listening, and the 10-minute break. Candidates who only drill isolated items often collapse at minute 70 of the real thing. Do at least two full runs.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: Night-before-the-test priorities?
o: Passport + confirmation ready, light review of structures, early sleep
questions.e: The night before is logistics + rest: documents laid out, centre route confirmed, light structural review (essay frame, SWT method), sleep by 10–11. Cramming new vocabulary now creates interference, not knowledge — and fatigue destroys fluency and listening the next morning.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: Morning-of-the-test routine?
o: Eat normally, arrive 30 minutes early, warm up your voice (read aloud 5 minutes) and ears (one dictation)
questions.e: Arrive 30 minutes early (late = no-show = fee lost), eat as usual, and warm up: 5 minutes of read-aloud primes fluency, one dictation primes the ear-hand loop. Excess caffeine + no food = shaky hands and racing speech. Boring routine, reliable performance.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: What is the biggest test-day mistake?
o: Technical zeros: silence past 3 seconds (mic closes), blank high-value items, wrong ID
questions.e: Technical zeros dwarf knowledge gaps: a closed mic on 3 speaking items, a blank WFD, or no-entry for wrong ID can cost 10–20 points — more than any vocabulary gap. Checklist before each part: mic test passed? 3-second rule armed? ID accepted? These are free points; don't donate them.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: How do institutions receive your scores?
o: You assign your score report to institutions through your myPTE account — free and unlimited
questions.e: myPTE lets you send score reports to institutions free and unlimited — no per-report fees, no mailing. Assign them only when applications are ready; reports stay valid 2 years. Never share your myPTE login to 'send' scores — assignment is a built-in feature.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: Your target is 79+ (competent English for Australian points). The honest assessment is:
o: Demanding: requires near-flawless WFD/SST/FIB, strong fluency, and error-free writing — plan 8–12 weeks
questions.e: 79+ is genuinely hard — it demands systematic preparation across 8–12 weeks for most learners: WFD near-perfect, SST/SWT polished, FIB strong, fluent unhesitant speaking, clean grammar. Template shortcuts and prediction banks are the two fastest ways to fall short of it in the 2026 scoring regime.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: What is a 'score plateau' and how do you break it?
o: A flat part of the test; skip it
Weeks of no improvement = the current method is exhausted; change the method (e.g. switch from templates to flexible structures, add dictation volume)
questions.e: Plateaus signal method exhaustion, not talent limits: if 4 weeks of template drills keep you at 58, the templates are the ceiling — switch to flexible frameworks + feedback. More of the same never breaks a plateau; different input does. A tutor or detailed Skills Profile review usually identifies the switch.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: Which free resources are genuinely sufficient for preparation?
o: Pearson's free practice + this site's banks + verified YouTube strategies + E2 free tier cover most needs; pay only for scored mocks
questions.e: The free stack is real: Pearson's official free practice, structured banks like this page, strategy videos from established channels, and free platform tiers. The one paid item worth buying is the official scored mock (real engine, real report). Coaching helps but is not mandatory — thousands of 79+ scorers are self-prepared.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: How far ahead should you book the test?
o: 2–4 weeks: enough for final preparation, with buffer to reschedule if mock scores aren't ready
questions.e: 2–4 weeks balances readiness and seat availability: close enough to be sharp, far enough to reschedule (fees apply within policy windows) if your scored mock says 'not yet'. Morning-of booking risks no seats; 6-month booking kills urgency.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: What should you do if the headset/mic malfunctions mid-test?
o: Raise your hand immediately — the invigilator logs it and you may get a remedy; never struggle silently
questions.e: Equipment issues are the centre's responsibility: raise your hand at once. The incident is logged, and Pearson can offer remedies (reschedule/retake) for documented faults. Silent struggling converts their problem into your score — and touching equipment yourself can void the session.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: True or False: you can choose the order of parts (e.g. do Listening first).
o: False — the order is fixed: Speaking & Writing, Reading, Listening
False — but you can skip parts
questions.e: Fixed order for everyone: Speaking & Writing → Reading → Listening, with the optional break after Reading. You cannot reorder, skip parts, or bank time across parts. Preparation must respect this sequence — practise full runs in order.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: What is the smartest use of your last 3 preparation days?
o: Taper: light timed drills on WFD/SST/FIB, one full dress-rehearsal mock, review structures — no new material
questions.e: Taper like an athlete: maintain sharpness with familiar drills, confirm timing in one final mock, review frameworks (essay, SWT, DI structure). New words/templates now create interference and anxiety. Confidence on test day comes from consolidated skill, not last-minute cramming.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: After the test, when and how do you get results?
o: Typically within 2 days via your myPTE account (email notification)
questions.e: Results typically land within 2 days in myPTE, with an email alert — then you view the full Score Report with the Skills Profile. Nothing is given at the centre. If results are delayed, check myPTE first; 'on hold' usually means a routine security review.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: Your friend says: 'Just memorise templates for every task.' Your 2026-informed reply?
o: 'Templates are now flagged by human reviewers on speaking/writing tasks — use flexible structures with real content instead.'
questions.e: The 2024–2026 scoring evolution (human content review on DI, RL, SGD, RTS; relevance scoring on writing) ended the template era. Flexible frameworks — same organisation, fresh content per prompt — give the structure without the flag. Memorised scripts are now the riskiest strategy in the test.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: What is the ONE habit that separates 65-scorers from 79-scorers?
o: Error elimination: 65-scorers know the methods; 79-scorers execute them without technical zeros, spelling slips, or form errors
questions.e: At 65 you know WHAT to do; at 79 you do it FLAWLESSLY: every WFD word spelt, every form window respected, no mic closures, no blank high-value items. The final 14 points are almost entirely error elimination — which is why checklists and proofread routines, not new tricks, close the gap.

questions.subject: Test Day & Strategy
questions.q: Final question: what is the correct mindset walking into the test centre?
o: 'Execute my procedures: 3-second rule, jot-and-type, checklists — the score follows the process.'
questions.e: Process over outcome: perfectionism creates the hesitation and panic that cause technical zeros; hope is not a strategy. Walk in with procedures — mic discipline, triage order, proofread scans — and execute them item by item. The score is a byproduct of 22 well-executed procedures.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Read Aloud items also count toward which other communicative skill?
questions.e: Read Aloud is an integrated task: it feeds both your Speaking score and your Reading score. That is why reading the text accurately matters as much as sounding fluent — misread words cost you on the Reading side too.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: In Read Aloud, the microphone closes automatically if you stay silent for how long?
questions.e: Three seconds of silence ends the recording. So if you lose your place, keep talking rather than pausing to find it — a wrong word costs less than a dead mic. Begin promptly when the status says Recording.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: You misread a word in Read Aloud. What should you do?
o: Pause, then re-read from the start
questions.e: Never backtrack. Corrections break your rhythm and hurt the Oral Fluency score far more than one misread word hurts Content. Pearson's own guidance: if you realise you made a mistake, continue speaking — fluency is scored on smoothness, not self-editing.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Which pace works best for Read Aloud?
o: As fast as possible to show fluency
questions.e: A natural, even pace with sensible phrase groups wins. Racing causes misreads (Content loss); crawling word-by-word sounds hesitant (Fluency loss). Aim for the rhythm of news reading — linked, unhurried, with light stress on key words.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: How should you use the 30–40 seconds of preparation time in Read Aloud?
o: Read the text silently, marking hard words and phrase breaks
questions.e: The mic is not live during prep, so read silently: spot difficult words, decide where phrases break, and note numbers or names. Reading aloud in prep wastes the advantage and can tire your voice before recording.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Which of these most damages the Pronunciation score in Read Aloud?
o: Mumbling word endings and swallowing syllables
questions.e: Accents are not penalised — the engine is trained on global Englishes. What hurts is unclear articulation: dropped endings (-ed, -s), swallowed syllables, and mumbling. Finish each word; consonant clarity matters more than accent.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: A Read Aloud text contains the number ‘1998’ and the term ‘CO₂’. How should you handle them?
questions.e: Render every token as speakable words: years as ‘nineteen ninety-eight’, CO₂ as ‘C-O-two’ (or ‘carbon dioxide’ if the text means that), % as ‘percent’. Decide during prep time so you never stall mid-recording.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: The Read Aloud text is 58 words long and your recording stops at 40 seconds. What happens?
o: Recording simply ends; you are scored on what you said
questions.e: 40 seconds is the hard cap — the recording stops and scoring proceeds on what you delivered. At a natural pace 50–60 words fit comfortably, so the cap only bites if you read far too slowly or restart.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: True or false: in Read Aloud, stressing important words and using sentence intonation improves your score.
o: True — it supports the Fluency score
True — but only for the Content score
questions.e: Natural stress and intonation are part of what the Oral Fluency trait measures — phrasing, rhythm and stress. Flat monotone reads as hesitant; lively-but-natural phrasing reads as fluent. Keep it newsreader-natural, not theatrical.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Why is Read Aloud considered a high-value task?
o: It is the easiest task in the test
It feeds two skill scores and appears 6–7 times
It is scored only by humans
questions.e: Six or seven items, each feeding both Speaking and Reading — no other task gives this much score per minute of effort. A candidate who masters RA lifts two of the four communicative scores at once, which is why preparation courses drill it first.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Your recording contains background noise from the test centre. What should you do?
o: Stop and ask the invigilator to move you
Speak slightly louder and keep a steady distance from the mic
questions.e: Centres are noisy by design — everyone speaks at once. Keep the mic at a fixed distance, speak at a clear steady volume, and do not touch it mid-item. The scoring engine is built to handle ambient speech; fiddling with the mic hurts more than the noise does.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Which preparation habit most improves Read Aloud scores over two weeks?
o: Reading news articles aloud daily with a timer
questions.e: Daily timed read-alouds of real articles build exactly the tested skill: accurate decoding at a fluent pace under time pressure. Model answers do not transfer because every item’s text is new; silent reading skips the pronunciation half of the task.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: In Read Aloud, what does the Content trait actually check?
o: Each word you said versus the text — correct, incorrect, or omitted
questions.e: Content is mechanical: every word in the text is marked correct, incorrect (misread/substituted), or omitted. Inserted extra words are ignored for content but can hurt fluency. Understanding the topic earns nothing extra — accuracy of reproduction is everything.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: A classmate says: ‘Skip difficult words in Read Aloud so your fluency stays smooth.’ What is wrong with this advice?
o: Skipped words count as omissions under Content, which also feeds Reading
questions.e: Every skipped word is an omission that lowers Content — and because RA feeds Reading, you lose twice. Better: attempt a close pronunciation and keep moving. One stumble costs a word; a skip costs a word plus signals hesitation.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: How close should you sit to the microphone for Read Aloud?
o: A fist’s width away, slightly below the mouth
questions.e: About a fist’s width, just below mouth level, kept still. Too close and plosives distort; too far and the engine strains to hear you. Test it in the unscored mic check at the start and then do not move it.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: The status bar shows ‘Beginning in: 5 seconds’ during Read Aloud prep. You have not finished reading the text. What now?
o: Start reading from the top at pace
Stay silent until you finish reading mentally
questions.e: When Recording starts you must speak. Starting from the top at a natural pace is the only scoring option — silence burns your 40 seconds and risks the 3-second auto-stop. This is why prep should prioritise the opening lines if time runs short.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Which pair of traits does the AI score on every Read Aloud response?
questions.e: RA is scored on three traits: Content (word accuracy), Oral Fluency (smoothness, phrasing, pace), and Pronunciation (clarity of sounds). Grammar and vocabulary are writing traits — they do not apply to read-aloud reproduction.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: You finish the text with 12 seconds of recording time left. What should you do?
o: Repeat the last sentence for emphasis
questions.e: Click Next. Silence risks nothing technically, but waiting wastes time you could bank for harder later tasks, and any stray noise could be captured. Repeating text adds nothing — extra words are simply ignored.

questions.subject: Read Aloud
questions.q: Why do teachers say Read Aloud is the best task for lifting a low Reading score?
o: Reading items are easier after speaking practice
Each RA item contributes directly to the Reading communicative score
questions.e: RA is one of the few tasks outside the Reading section that feeds the Reading score — with 6–7 items, it is a large chunk of your Reading evidence. Candidates weak at FIB-Reading often gain more Reading points from RA accuracy than from extra reading drills.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: A Repeat Sentence recording plays once and lasts about 9 seconds. How long do you have to repeat it?
questions.e: You get 15 seconds after the 3-second countdown. That is generous for a 3–9 second sentence — the challenge is memory, not time. Start speaking as soon as the mic opens; hesitation eats the window and risks the auto-stop.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Repeat Sentence scoring gives 3 points for a perfect repeat. How many points for getting just over half the words right?
questions.e: Content is banded: 3 = all words correct in order, 2 = more than 50% correct, 1 = less than 50% but something right, 0 = nothing usable. Fluency and pronunciation add up to 5 more points per item, so even a partial repeat spoken smoothly earns well.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: You remember only the first half of a Repeat Sentence. What is the best strategy?
o: Stay silent — partial answers score zero
Say the half you remember, fluently
questions.e: Say what you remember and say it smoothly. A half-correct fluent repeat earns Content 1 plus solid Fluency/Pronunciation points; silence earns zero everywhere. Inventing words adds errors, and stalling risks the 3-second cutoff.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Repeat Sentence feeds which two communicative scores?
questions.e: Repeat Sentence is integrated: Speaking (fluency, pronunciation, content) and Listening (you must decode the audio accurately). It appears 10–12 times, making it the highest-volume speaking task — a top priority for score gain.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: What is the most practical note-taking method during a Repeat Sentence recording?
o: Jot initials of content words as you listen
Write the sentence after it plays
questions.e: You cannot write full sentences in 3–9 seconds, but capturing the initials of content words (nouns, verbs) gives your memory anchors to rebuild from. Full transcription is impossible at natural speech speed and splits your attention.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: The speaker says ‘The university library will close at 6 pm on Fridays.’ You say ‘The university library will close at 6 pm on Friday.’ How is this scored?
o: It depends on the examiner’s mood
questions.e: Content scoring is word-form exact: ‘Friday’ ≠ ‘Fridays’. Meaning does not rescue it — plurals, tenses and articles all count. Train your ear on endings (-s, -ed) because they are the most commonly lost points.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Describe Image gives you 25 seconds to study the image. What should you prioritise?
o: The overall trend/relationship plus 2–3 key figures
questions.e: Content rewards describing key relationships, trends and extremes — not reciting the whole dataset. Grab the headline pattern (rose/fell/peaked, highest/lowest) and two or three anchor numbers; a perfect inventory spoken hesitantly scores worse than a clear summary.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Which template structure works reliably for Describe Image?
o: Introduction → key features with data → conclusion
List every label left to right
Give your opinion on the topic
questions.e: The classic three-part frame — what the image shows, 2–3 key features with numbers, and a concluding trend — guarantees 35–40 seconds of organised speech. Opinions and design commentary earn no content points; the scorer wants data relationships.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: You get a Describe Image with an unfamiliar chart type. What should you do?
o: Stay silent — you cannot describe what you do not understand
Apply the same template: title, axes, highest/lowest, trend, conclusion
questions.e: The template is chart-agnostic: read the title, name the variables, pick the highest and lowest values, state any visible trend, conclude. Fluency and pronunciation are scored regardless of chart type, so a calm generic description beats silence every time.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: True or false: since late 2024, Describe Image and Retell Lecture responses are also reviewed by human scorers.
o: True — they are double-scored by AI plus human
False — only essays get human review
questions.e: Pearson moved DI and RL to double scoring: the AI engine plus human expert review of content. Practically, this means template-only waffle with no real content is riskier than before — the human checks whether you actually described the image.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: In Describe Image, you run out of things to say after 25 seconds. What saves the response?
o: Comparing two data points, restating the trend, or projecting implications
questions.e: Stretch with content: compare the highest vs lowest, restate the trend in new words, note an exception. Never announce you are finished — fill the 40 seconds with relevant speech. Silence after 25 seconds reads as a breakdown in fluency.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: Which error hurts a Describe Image response most?
questions.e: A 3-second silence can end the recording entirely — catastrophic. Mispronunciations and simple words cost a point here and there; a dead mic ends the item. Keep air moving: filler-free continuous speech is the golden rule of all PTE speaking.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: For Repeat Sentence, why do experts say ‘chunking’ helps?
o: It lets you skip hard words
Grouping words into meaning phrases (3–4 chunks) fits short-term memory better than 12 loose words
questions.e: Short-term memory holds about 4 chunks, not 12 words. Hearing ‘The new policy / will affect / international students / from next semester’ as four ideas lets you rebuild the sentence even if exact words blur. Practise by repeating news headlines in phrases.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: A process diagram appears in Describe Image. What is the best opening line?
questions.e: Name the process immediately: ‘This diagram illustrates the stages of water recycling.’ Then walk through the stages in order with linking words (first, next, finally). Opinions and vague openers waste the high-attention first seconds.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: How many Describe Image items appear, and how long is each response?
questions.e: Expect 3–4 images with 25 seconds of prep and 40 seconds to speak. Forty seconds is plenty for intro + key features + conclusion — most underperformance comes from running dry at 20 seconds, not from time pressure.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: In Repeat Sentence, the audio includes ‘might have been’ and you say ‘might be’. What is the damage?
o: You lose those content words; contractions and auxiliaries all count
questions.e: Every word form counts, including little grammar words: ‘have’ and ‘been’ are two lost content words. Weak forms (contractions, auxiliaries, prepositions) are exactly what untrained ears drop — shadow native speech to catch them.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: What is ‘shadowing’ and why do PTE coaches recommend it for Repeat Sentence?
o: Repeating audio with a 1-second delay, mimicking rhythm and sounds
questions.e: Shadowing = speaking along just behind a native speaker, copying stress, linking and weak forms in real time. Ten minutes daily rewires your ear-mouth loop for exactly what RS tests: instant accurate reproduction of natural speech.

questions.subject: Repeat Sentence & Describe Image
questions.q: A bar chart in Describe Image has no clear trend — values just differ. What do you describe?
o: Say there is no trend and stop
Rank the categories: highest, lowest, notable gaps
questions.e: No trend is fine — ranking is content: ‘X is highest at 45%, nearly double Y, the lowest at 23%.’ Comparisons, ratios and extremes are all scorable content. Never invent movement the data does not show; the human reviewer will notice.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Retell Lecture: the lecture can run up to 90 seconds. How much preparation time do you get before speaking?
questions.e: You get 10 seconds after the audio ends before the mic opens, then 40 seconds to retell. Ten seconds is for glancing at your notes and picking your opening line — the real work (note-taking) happens during the lecture itself.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Which note-taking method suits Retell Lecture best?
o: Keywords, numbers and arrows linking ideas
questions.e: Capture content words, figures and relationships with arrows — you cannot write sentences at lecture speed. Aim for 8–12 key terms that let you rebuild the talk’s skeleton: topic, 2–3 main points, one striking detail or number.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Retell Lecture feeds which two communicative scores?
questions.e: Retell Lecture is integrated like the other long speaking tasks: Speaking (fluency, pronunciation, content) plus Listening (accurate capture of the lecture). With only 1–2 items, each one carries serious weight — notes are non-negotiable.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Your 40-second retell covers the lecture’s main points but misses one minor example. How bad is this?
o: Minor — content rewards key points and relationships, not exhaustive detail
questions.e: Content scoring looks for the lecture’s key ideas and their relationships. A dropped minor example costs little; a dropped main argument costs a lot. Prioritise the skeleton (thesis + main points) over decorative details when notes are thin.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Which opening works best for a Retell Lecture response?
o: ‘The lecture was about…’ followed by the topic in your own words
Repeating the lecturer’s first sentence verbatim
questions.e: State the topic immediately in your own words, then the main points with linkers. Paraphrasing demonstrates comprehension (and dodges any over-reliance on memorised chunks); apologising or opining wastes prime seconds.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: True or false: in Retell Lecture, using the exact phrases from the lecture maximises your content score.
o: True — exact wording maximises the content score
False — key ideas matter, and paraphrase is fine
True — but only for the fluency score
False — quoting the lecture is penalised
questions.e: Content is about ideas, not quotation. Paraphrasing the main points scores just as well and is safer — verbatim recall of 90 seconds of speech is unreliable, and half-remembered quotes derail fluency. Capture meaning, not wording.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: The lecture is on an unfamiliar technical topic. What is your best move?
o: Stay silent — you cannot retell what you did not understand
Retell the structure: topic, what the speaker emphasised, any numbers/names caught
Guess the topic from one word
Talk about a related topic you know
questions.e: Even partial capture earns points: the topic area, repeated terms, numbers, and the speaker’s stance (‘argued that…’, ‘compared X with Y’). Going off-topic earns zero content; structured partial recall earns real marks plus full fluency credit for smooth delivery.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: How should you distribute the 40 seconds in Retell Lecture?
questions.e: A mini-talk structure: topic sentence, two or three points with linkers, one-line wrap-up. This fills the time with organised content and avoids the two classic failures — drying up at 15 seconds or rambling on one point.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Answer Short Question: you hear ‘What do you call the frozen form of water?’ — how should you answer?
o: ‘The frozen form of water is called ice.’
Stay silent — too easy to be real
questions.e: One or two words, immediately. ASQ is scored on vocabulary correctness only — a single correct word earns the point, and a full sentence wastes your 10 seconds and risks nothing gained. Do not overthink easy items; they are genuinely easy.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: How is Answer Short Question scored?
questions.e: ASQ is pure vocabulary: right word(s) = 1 point, wrong = 0. Fluency and pronunciation are not scored, so mumbling the right word still scores. This makes ASQ the cheapest points in the speaking section — answer every item, even with a guess.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: You do not know the answer to an Answer Short Question. What should you do?
questions.e: Guess a related word — there is no penalty for wrong answers and no negative marking. Silence guarantees zero; a related guess sometimes lands. ‘I don’t know’ is always wrong, and repeats are not offered.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Answer Short Question moved sections in the 2025 test update. Where does it sit now?
o: In the Speaking section, after Retell Lecture
questions.e: Since the 2025 update, Answer Short Question sits in the Speaking section (Part 1) rather than Listening. Expect 5–6 quick items — 10 seconds each, one or a few words. The scoring did not change: vocabulary correctness only.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Which of these is the best daily drill for Answer Short Question?
questions.e: ASQ tests instant retrieval of common nouns and facts under a 10-second clock. Timed one-word-answer flashcards build exactly that reflex. Novels and films build passive knowledge too slowly for the format’s speed demand.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: ‘What instrument is used to measure temperature?’ — which answer gets the point?
o: The device that measures how hot or cold something is
questions.e: The expected term ‘thermometer’. ASQ accepts the standard word or a close equivalent the scoring key lists — but circumlocutions and related-but-wrong words (‘degree’, ‘hot’) do not match. Learn the canonical one-word labels for common concepts.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: In Retell Lecture, the speaker says ‘photosynthesis’ five times. You cannot spell it in notes. What do you do?
o: Stop listening to work out the spelling
Write it phonetically and keep listening
questions.e: Notes are for you, not the scorer — phonetic scribbles (‘fotosinth’) are fine. Never sacrifice listening time to perfect a note; the idea chain matters more than any single term. Capture and continue.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: Why do coaches call Retell Lecture ‘Describe Image with audio’?
o: Both need the same skill: extract key points under time pressure and deliver a structured 40-second talk
questions.e: The delivery skill transfers directly: topic sentence, key points with linkers, conclusion, 40 seconds, no 3-second silences. The only new skill is note-taking under audio pressure — the speaking frame is one you already own from Describe Image.

questions.subject: Retell Lecture & Answer Short Q
questions.q: A Retell Lecture response that lists points without linking words will mainly lose marks on…
questions.e: Choppy unlinked listing sounds hesitant and disjointed — a fluency hit. Linkers (however, moreover, as a result) create the smooth connected speech the fluency trait rewards. Content may survive, but the delivery score bleeds.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: Your SWT sentence is 80 words long. What is the consequence?
o: Form score of zero for the item
It is fine — up to 100 words allowed
Only the extra words are ignored
questions.e: Form requires 5–75 words in exactly one sentence; breaching either gives zero for Form. At 80 words you fail the word-count rule outright. Draft to ~60 words, then count before submitting — you have 10 minutes, use two for checking.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: Which sentence correctly follows SWT form?
o: ‘The study shows X. It also shows Y.’
‘The study shows X, and it also shows Y.’
questions.e: One sentence only — clauses joined by ‘and’ with a single capital and single full stop. Two sentences, even short ones, fail Form and zero the item. Fragments and scrambled word order fail grammar too.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: What is the most reliable SWT method taught by preparation courses?
o: Copy the first and last sentences
Find the main idea + 2–3 key supporting points, then compress into one complex sentence
Write your opinion of the passage
questions.e: Identify the thesis and the two or three load-bearing points, then fuse them with subordinate clauses (‘although…, because…, which…’). Copying sentences risks plagiarism-thin content scores; opinions score zero content.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: SWT is scored on which four traits?
questions.e: SWT traits: Content (key points captured), Form (one sentence, 5–75 words), Grammar (correct complex sentence), Vocabulary (appropriate academic word choice). Fluency and pronunciation are speaking traits — irrelevant here.

questions.subject: Summarize Written Text
questions.q: You have written your SWT sentence with 3 minutes left. Best use of the time?
o: Count the words, check it is one sentence, fix articles and verb forms
Add a second sentence for detail
